entry.title: New AI Features in SAP Enterprise Threat Detection, Cloud Edition
entry.content:
Security investigations are often complex and time-consuming. Monitoring agents must sift through vast amounts of log data, evaluate the risk posed by individual ABAP objects, and translate technical findings into clear, actionable recommendations.

Since August we've introduced three AI-assisted features in SAP Enterprise Threat Detection, cloud edition that help monitoring agents work more efficiently: Behavior analysis, criticality assessments for ABAP objects, and recommendation templates.

Let's take a closer look at what's new.

Behavior analysis: Let AI surface suspicious activity for you

When an investigation is underway and you've identified suspicious users through alerts, the harder question surfaces: what exactly did they do, and how serious was it? Manually reviewing large volumes of log data to answer that takes time you often don't have.

That's where behavior analysis comes in. From the Behavior Analysis tab on the investigation details page, you can trigger an AI-powered analysis of the users already linked to your investigation—without leaving your current context. The AI examines their activity across your event data and returns a list of suspicious log events, each tagged with a severity level (Very High, High, Medium, or Low) and an explanation of the AI's reasoning. You can then select individual events and assign them to your investigation as evidence.

 What you'll need: The UEBAManager role and accepted SAP AI Terms and Conditions

For more information, see Running a Behavior Analysis | SAP Help Portal.


Criticality information for ABAP objects: Know your risk at a glance

Not every ABAP object carries the same risk — but assessing that risk manually takes expertise and time. AI-assisted criticality assessments are now available for four ABAP object types: HTTP paths, function modules, transactions, and reports.

The assessment is available directly within the apps where you already work as a monitoring agent: Analyze Log Events, Manage Value Lists, Manage Investigations, and Manage Alerts. When you request criticality information for an object, the system returns:

  • A criticality level (Very High, High, Medium, Low, or Unknown)
  • A plain-language explanation of why the object is security-critical
  • Remediation recommendations to reduce the risk
  • Where applicable, details about relevant SAP Security Notes, including CVSS scores and publication dates

A feedback option lets you flag inaccurate or misleading AI-generated content helping improve results over time.

What you'll need: The roles CriticalObjectsAIManager and accepted SAP AI Terms and Conditions.

For more information, see Criticality Information for ABAP Objects | SAP Help Portal.

 

AI-assisted recommendation templates: Faster, more consistent investigation reports

When closing an investigation, monitoring agents write a recommendation for the customer — what happened, why it matters, and what to do next. Getting that right, consistently, across many different patterns, can be a challenge.

We've made it easier with AI-assisted recommendation templates. In the Manage Patterns app, you can now use a chat interface to describe the template you need, and the system generates a structured draft. You can then refine it through the chat or edit it directly before saving.

Each template follows a clear three-part structure: what happened (investigation result), why it matters (alert reason), and what to do (recommended action). Placeholders in the template are automatically filled with real event data when a monitoring agent generates a recommendation for a specific investigation.

You can create templates at two levels: global templates that apply across all tenants, and tenant-specific templates. SAP-provided templates for standard patterns are also available to view as a reference.

What you'll need: The roles CriticalObjectsAIManager and CrossTenantCriticalObjectsManager and accepted SAP AI Terms and Conditions.

For more information, see Creating Recommendation Templates | SAP Help Portal.

 

Wrapping up

These three features reflect a broader direction we're taking with SAP Enterprise Threat Detection: putting AI where it reduces friction in security work. Behavior analysis helps you focus on the activities that matter most. Criticality assessments give you instant context on risky ABAP objects without having to dig through documentation. And AI-assisted recommendation templates help you produce clearer, more consistent reports in less time.

Together, these innovations help security teams make better-informed decisions and respond faster to potential threats.

entry.title: Quantum-Safe by Default: How SAP S/4HANA Closes the Door on Harvest Now, Decrypt Later Attacks
entry.content:
Quantum computing is no longer a distant theoretical concern — it is an active security planning challenge with real implications for how SAP landscapes protect data today. With the latest release of the SAP Cryptographic Library, SAP has taken a significant step forward: post-quantum key exchange is now available for S/4HANA across all deployment models, as well as for BAIP ABAP Environment. Here is what you need to know.

The Quantum Threat to Public Key Cryptography

Modern public key cryptography — the foundation of secure communication on the internet and inside enterprise systems — rests on mathematical problems that are computationally infeasible for classical computers. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers. Elliptic Curve Cryptography and Diffie-Hellman key exchange rely on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem. These properties have made them the workhorses of TLS, digital signatures, and key exchange for decades.

Quantum computers change this calculus fundamentally. In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor published an algorithm that solves both integer factorization and the discrete logarithm problem in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) running Shor's algorithm could break RSA, ECDHE, and ECDSA — not in thousands of years as with classical brute-force attacks, but in hours or even minutes.

It is important to be precise: today's quantum computers are not yet capable of this. They are too small and error-prone to threaten production key sizes. But the trajectory of progress — more qubits, better error correction, and increasingly efficient implementations of Shor's algorithm — means that the question is not whether a CRQC will emerge, but when. Most credible estimates place that window somewhere in the next one to two decades, with some more recent research suggesting the timelines may be shorter than previously assumed.

The consequence is that any system still relying solely on RSA, ECDHE, or similar classical algorithms at that point will have no meaningful protection for the confidentiality of its communications.

Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why the Clock Is Already Running

One might reasonably ask: if CRQCs do not yet exist, why act now? The answer lies in a threat strategy already being executed by sophisticated adversaries today, known as Harvest Now, Decrypt Later.

The attack is conceptually simple but strategically powerful. An adversary intercepts and archives encrypted network traffic today. The data cannot be read yet, but it does not need to be. It is stored and held in reserve until a capable quantum computer becomes available. At that point, the attacker uses Shor's algorithm to recover the session keys from the classical key exchange, and retroactively decrypts all the stored ciphertext.

This means the exposure occurs at the moment of transmission, not at the moment of decryption. Any data transmitted today under a purely classical key exchange is potentially at risk if it must remain confidential for a decade or more — and there is growing evidence that threat actors are actively collecting this data right now.

The implication for enterprise systems is clear: sensitive business data, financial transactions, intellectual property, and HR records that travel over TLS-protected connections today may be in an attacker's archive already. Waiting until CRQCs are publicly available to migrate to post-quantum cryptography is, by definition, too late for that data.

This is precisely why the focus of early post-quantum migration is on key exchange rather than digital signatures. Key exchange is the mechanism that protects data confidentiality in transit, and it is the vector that Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks exploit. Migrating to quantum-safe key exchange now ensures that traffic captured today cannot be decrypted by a future quantum adversary — even if they are storing it as you read this.

Post-Quantum Key Exchange Is Now Available for S/4HANA and BAIP ABAP Environment

SAP has taken a concrete step toward quantum-safe communications with the release of the SAP Cryptographic Library (a.k.a  CommonCryptoLib, CCL) version 8.6.2. This version introduces support for a hybrid post-quantum TLS 1.3 handshake — specifically, a hybrid key agreement based on X25519MLKEM768, which combines the classical X25519 elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange with ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-based Key Encapsulation Mechanism), the algorithm standardized by NIST as FIPS 203.

The hybrid approach is deliberate and follows the industry best practice for this transition period: by combining a classical and a post-quantum key exchange in parallel, the resulting session key is secure as long as either of the two algorithms remains unbroken. This gives you quantum resistance against Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks today, while retaining the proven security of classical cryptography.

This capability is available across all S/4HANA deployment models:

  • S/4HANA Public Cloud
  • S/4HANA Private Cloud
  • S/4HANA On-Premise

Additionally, it is also available on the following BAIP environment:

  • BAIP ABAP Environment

Prerequisites

Two prerequisites must be in place:

  1. SAP Cryptographic Library 8.6.2 or higher — to enable ML-KEM support in the TLS handshake.
  2. A TLS 1.3-compatible SAP Kernel — TLS 1.3 is a strict prerequisite for the post-quantum key exchange. All S/4HANA Public Cloud kernels, as well as the kernel of BAIP ABAP Environment, are compatible and have TLS 1.3 enabled by default. For Private Cloud and On-Premise systems, please see SAP Note 3318423 for the required SAP Kernel versions and patch levels.

Plug and Play Activation

Once both prerequisites are satisfied, no additional configuration is required. The post-quantum hybrid key exchange activates automatically for all TLS 1.3 connections. There is no switch to flip and no profile parameter to set. When a TLS 1.3 connection is established between two endpoints that both support X25519MLKEM768, the hybrid key agreement happens transparently.

This plug-and-play behavior significantly lowers the barrier to adoption: upgrading your SAP Cryptographic Library and ensuring your kernel is TLS 1.3-capable is all it takes to bring post-quantum protection to your S/4HANA system’s TLS protected communication channels.

Potential Issues with Third-Party TLS Connections

While the hybrid post-quantum key exchange works seamlessly between SAP components, connections to third-party systems and external services may require attention.

The root cause is a practical one: ML-KEM key exchange values are significantly larger than those produced by classical ECDHE. A standard ECDHE key share is a few dozen bytes; an ML-KEM key share (as used in X25519MLKEM768) is several kilobytes. Not all TLS implementations handle these larger payloads correctly — some may fail the handshake, reject the connection, or behave unpredictably when they encounter a key share size they were not designed for.

If you observe TLS handshake failures or unexpected connection drops to third-party systems after upgrading to CCL 8.6.2 or higher, the post-quantum key size is a likely contributing factor. The recommended remediation is to disable post-quantum key exchange selectively for those specific connections using session-specific cipher suite configuration rather than disabling it globally.

Public Cloud: Communication System Settings

In S/4HANA Public Cloud and BAIP ABAP Environment, profile parameters are not directly accessible. For outbound connections to third-party systems that cannot handle TLS 1.3's post-quantum key sizes, the recommended approach is to disable TLS 1.3 for that specific connection via the Cipher Suites attribute of the Communication System configuration in the SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud and SAP BAIP administration tools. Configuring the communication system to use TLS 1.2 for the affected destination ensures interoperability while limiting the scope of the restriction to only the affected endpoint.

Learn more about Communication System configuration on the SAP Help Portal page How to Create Communication Systems. 

On-Premise and Private Cloud: SM59 Configuration

For RFC and HTTP connections configured via SM59, you can override the TLS cipher suite string on a per-destination basis using the TLS Cipher Suites field on the Logon & Security tab of a type G or H destination. This allows you to target only the affected connection without touching the system-wide profile parameters.

In comparison to Public Cloud systems, where the post-quantum key exchange can only be disabled indirectly via disabling of TLS 1.3, the configuration via SM59 allows for ML-KEM to be disabled directly, leaving TLS 1.3 otherwise intact. This can be done by adjusting the cipher suite string to exclude the ML-KEM-based key exchange group. The exact syntax and the correct cipher suite string to use for this purpose are described in SAP Note 3346659, Section 3.7.

For full documentation on how the TLS Cipher Suites field works in SM59 and how session-specific cipher suite overrides interact with system-wide settings, refer to the SAP Help Portal page Field <TLS Cipher Suites>.

Conclusion

Post-quantum key exchange in S/4HANA is not a future roadmap item — it is available today, and the case for deploying it promptly is compelling. The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later threat means that data traversing your landscape right now may already be targeted by adversaries banking on future quantum decryption capabilities. With SAP Cryptographic Library 8.6.2 or higher and a TLS 1.3-compatible kernel, you can close that window with minimal operational effort. The hybrid X25519MLKEM768 approach delivers quantum-safe key exchange as a drop-in capability, and targeted cipher suite configuration via SM59 or Communication System settings allows you to manage any third-party compatibility edge cases without compromising the broader security posture of your landscape.

Further Information

  • SAP Note 3685428 - Fixes and features in CommonCryptoLib 8.6.2
  • SAP Note 3318423 - Is TLS 1.3 Supported by SAP Kernel for ABAP and SAP S/4HANA?
  • SAP Note 3532801 - Support for TLS 1.3 -- Downport for SAP AS ABAP Kernel
  • SAP Note 3346659 - TLS Ciphersuite String Configuration for SAP AS ABAP Systems and for SAP Kernel Software Components - Section 3.7
  • How to Create Communication Systems | SAP Help Portal
  • Configure TLS Attributes in SM59 | SAP Help Portal

entry.title: SNC with Kerberos after migration, Part 2: Oracle 19c, the dynamic linker and LD_PRELOAD
entry.content:
Introduction

About this series. After a data center migration to RHEL 9 and an Oracle 19c client, our SAP ABAP system would not start once SNC with Kerberos was switched on. Behind that one symptom were two separate problems. This series walks through them one part at a time:

  • Overview: the whole story and both fixes in short
  • Part 1: how SNC with Kerberos logs you into SAP without a password
  • Part 2 (this post): why the Oracle 19c client crashed the work process, the dynamic linker and LD_PRELOAD
  • Part 3: how I proved it, the traces, the checks and the dead ends
  • Part 4: "Initiating Credentials not available": keytab, ticket and credential cache
  • Part 5: runbook and cheat sheet

In Part 1 I explained how SNC with Kerberos works, using a normal VDI login as the example. This post goes deep into the first and stranger of the two problems: the work process aborted right after SAP had loaded the Kerberos library successfully. The cause was not in SAP and not in Kerberos. It was in the way Linux connects programs to their libraries.

The symptom

With snc/enable = 0 the system started normally. With snc/enable = 1 the work processes died during startup. The trace looked fine at first:

N  SncInit(): Initializing Secure Network Communication (SNC)
N  SncInit(): found  snc/gssapi_lib=/usr/lib64/libgssapi_krb5.so
N    File "/usr/lib64/libgssapi_krb5.so" dynamically loaded as GSS-API v2 library.

Then the process received SIGABRT. The stack, read from the bottom up:

/usr/lib64/libc.so.6 (abort)
<ORACLE_HOME>/lib/libclntsh.so.11.1 (krb5int_key_register)
<ORACLE_HOME>/lib/libclntsh.so.11.1 (gss_krb5int_lib_init)
SncPDLInit()
SncInit()
ThSncInit()

SAP started SNC, SNC started Kerberos, and the Kerberos start-up code was running inside libclntsh.so, the Oracle client library. That was the moment I stopped looking at SNC parameters and started looking at libraries.

A small trap on the way: the file is called libclntsh.so.11.1, but it is the 19c client. Oracle keeps that old file name for compatibility, so the name tells you nothing about the version.

One Linux concept you need: the dynamic linker

A program like the SAP work process does not contain all of its code. It calls functions by name, and the code for those names lives in shared libraries, the .so files. The Oracle client is one, MIT Kerberos is another, the SAP Cryptographic Library is a third.

When a process starts, and whenever it loads a library later on demand, a part of Linux called the dynamic linker loads these libraries and connects each function name to real code. SAP loads the library from snc/gssapi_lib on demand, when SNC starts.

The important rule: all libraries in one process share one list of names, and the linker searches that list in load order. The first library that offers a name wins.

Analogy: think of an office with one phone directory. Every department that moves in writes its people into the directory, in the order they arrive. When someone calls and asks for "Raj", the receptionist looks from the top and connects the first Raj she finds. If two departments both have a Raj, the second one never gets a call meant for him.

What was inside the Oracle client

Running nm on the Oracle client lists the function names it offers to the rest of the process:

nm -D <ORACLE_HOME>/lib/libclntsh.so.11.1 | grep -E 'gss_krb5int|krb5int'

gss_krb5int_lib_init
gss_krb5int_initialize_library
krb5int_key_register
krb5int_cc_default
krb5int_accessor
...

These are internal functions of MIT Kerberos. Normally only MIT Kerberos itself uses them. The Oracle 19c client carries its own copy of this code and makes the names visible to everyone in the process.

In the phone directory picture: the Oracle department brought its own people called gss_krb5int_lib_init and krb5int_key_register, and the MIT Kerberos department has people with exactly the same names.

What happened inside one work process

  1. The work process starts and connects to the database. To do that it loads the Oracle client. Oracle's names, including its Kerberos copies, are written into the directory first.
  2. SNC starts and loads MIT Kerberos from snc/gssapi_lib, together with its helper libraries. The load itself works, which is why the trace says "dynamically loaded".
  3. MIT Kerberos initializes itself and calls its own internal function gss_krb5int_lib_init.
  4. The linker looks up the name, finds Oracle's copy first, and sends the call there.
  5. Oracle's copy calls krb5int_key_register, again Oracle's copy, and finds internal state that MIT's half had set up differently. The two halves do not match.
  6. Kerberos notices the inconsistency and calls abort(). SIGABRT, the work process dies, the instance does not come up.

SIGABRT is worth a second look. It is not a segmentation fault, where code touches bad memory. It means the code checked something, found it wrong and stopped itself on purpose. That fits two copies of the same library tripping over each other's state.

<

Why the old system never had this problem

  Old system (SLES, Oracle 11g client) New system (RHEL 9, Oracle 19c client)

snc/gssapi_libMIT libgssapi_krb5.soMIT libgssapi_krb5.so
Oracle client exports MIT Kerberos internalsNoYes
Result with SNC onWorksSIGABRT

Same SAP configuration, same MIT Kerberos. Only the Oracle client changed. With 11g there was nothing in the directory to collide with.

Why the sqlnet.ora change did not help

My first idea was that Oracle wanted to use Kerberos for its own database login, so I set SQLNET.AUTHENTICATION_SERVICES = (NONE) in sqlnet.ora. Nothing changed, and I reverted it.

Looking back, it could not help. That setting controls whether Oracle uses Kerberos to log in. The clash happens simply because Oracle's library sits in the process and offers those names. A runtime setting cannot change which copy the linker picks.

The fix: LD_PRELOAD

LD_PRELOAD is an environment variable that tells the linker: load these libraries before everything else. Their names go to the top of the directory, so they win every lookup, including lookups made from inside other libraries.

I added this to the profile of the <sid>adm user:

export LD_PRELOAD=/lib64/libgssapi_krb5.so.2:/lib64/libkrb5.so.3:/lib64/libk5crypto.so.3:/lib64/libkrb5support.so.0

The four libraries are the MIT Kerberos stack:

  • libgssapi_krb5.so.2: the GSS-API layer that SNC talks to, home of gss_krb5int_lib_init
  • libkrb5.so.3: the Kerberos protocol itself
  • libk5crypto.so.3: the encryption routines
  • libkrb5support.so.0: internal helpers, home of krb5int_key_register

Environment variables are read when a process starts. The work processes are started by sapstartsrv, not by your shell, so a full stop and start of the instance is needed, including sapstartsrv. After that, the crash was gone.

In the phone directory picture: the MIT Kerberos department now moves in before anyone else, so every call for its people reaches the right person. Oracle's copies are still in the file, but nobody calls them any more. Database access is not affected, because Oracle does not use Kerberos for its login here.

Things to keep in mind

  • LD_PRELOAD applies to everything started as <sid>adm, including lsnrctl, sqlplus and the BR*Tools. That was fine for us because Oracle does not use Kerberos authentication on this database.
  • After operating system patches, check that the four preloaded files still exist under the same names.
  • If Oracle Kerberos authentication is switched on for the database later, test this setup again.
  • I did not find a SAP Note that describes this exact combination. If you know one, please add it in the comments.

How to check if you have the same problem

# 1. Does the crash stack show Kerberos functions inside the Oracle client?
grep -A20 -i "abort" /usr/sap/<SID>/D*/work/dev_w0

# 2. Does your Oracle client export MIT Kerberos internals?
nm -D <ORACLE_HOME>/lib/libclntsh.so* | grep -E 'gss_krb5int|krb5int'

# 3. After the fix, is LD_PRELOAD set for the SAP user?
echo $LD_PRELOAD

If the first two show Kerberos names inside libclntsh.so, you most likely have the same clash.

Conclusion and what is next

The crash was a clash between two copies of Kerberos in one process: the one inside the Oracle 19c client and the real MIT Kerberos. LD_PRELOAD makes sure the real one is found first. If you see Kerberos functions inside libclntsh.so in a crash stack, start there, not with the SNC parameters.

With the crash fixed, SNC got one step further and stopped at "Initiating Credentials not available". Part 3 shows how I worked through both problems: reading the traces, comparing with the old system, and the checks that turned out to be dead ends. I will add the link here once it is published.

Follow me here on SAP Community to get notified when the next part comes out. And if you have seen Oracle or another library bring its own copy of Kerberos into an SAP process, tell me in the comments how you handled it.

entry.title: SNC with Kerberos after migration, Part 3: how I proved it, and the dead ends
entry.content:
Introduction

About this series. After a data center migration to RHEL 9 and an Oracle 19c client, our SAP ABAP system would not start once SNC with Kerberos was switched on. Behind that one symptom were two separate problems.

  • Overview: the whole story and both fixes in short
  • Part 1: how SNC with Kerberos logs you into SAP without a password
  • Part 2: why the Oracle 19c client crashed the work process, and LD_PRELOAD
  • Part 3 (this post): how I proved it, and the dead ends
  • Part 4: "Initiating Credentials not available": keytab, ticket and credential cache
  • Part 5: runbook and cheat sheet

Parts 1 and 2 explain what was wrong. This short post is about how I got there: five checks, in the order I did them, and the ones that led nowhere. The method works for any SNC startup problem, not only this one.

1. Read the trace from the bottom up

The work process trace (dev_w*) tells you two things: how far SAP got, and where it stopped. Mine said SAP had loaded the Kerberos library successfully, and then the stack ended in abort() inside libclntsh.so, the Oracle client.

That one line moved the search away from SNC parameters. If SAP had failed to load the library, the problem would be the path. It loaded fine, so the problem was what happened after.

2. Clear the simple configuration errors first

The very first start failed for a boring reason: the profile still pointed snc/gssapi_lib to an old Quest library that did not exist on the new server. dlopen failed with "No such file or directory".

Lesson: after a migration, check every path in the SNC parameters before you look for anything clever.

3. Compare with a system that works

Our old production system ran the same SNC setup for years. I put the two side by side:

  Old (works) New (crashes)

snc/gssapi_libMIT KerberosMIT Kerberos
SAP Cryptographic Library loadedYesYes
Oracle client11g19c
LinuxSLESRHEL 9

Same SNC configuration, same Kerberos library. Only the Oracle client and the operating system had changed, so those were the two suspects.

4. Prove it with nm

A stack trace shows where code ran. nm shows which library owns a function name. Two commands settled it:

nm -D <ORACLE_HOME>/lib/libclntsh.so* | grep -E 'gss_krb5int|krb5int'
# returns MIT Kerberos internal functions: Oracle carries its own copy

nm -D /usr/sap/<SID>/SYS/exe/run/libsapcrypto.so | grep -i krb
# returns nothing: the SAP Cryptographic Library has no Kerberos code

Now the evidence matched: the Oracle 19c client offers the same Kerberos function names as MIT Kerberos, and the stack showed MIT's start-up landing in Oracle's copy. Part 2 explains why that crashes.

5. Treat the next error as progress

After LD_PRELOAD fixed the crash, SNC stopped with a new message: "Initiating Credentials krb5 not available". It is tempting to think the fix failed. It had not. SAP simply got one step further and hit the next problem. Accepting was OK, initiating was not, which pointed straight at a missing ticket. That is Part 4.

The dead ends

  • Keytab and Kerberos ports. The first reply to my SAP Community question suggested checking these. Good first checks, but both were fine. The library loaded and the accepting credential worked, which already proves the keytab is readable.
  • sqlnet.ora. I set SQLNET.AUTHENTICATION_SERVICES = (NONE), thinking Oracle wanted Kerberos for its own login. No change. It controls Oracle's login method, not which copy of a function the linker picks.
  • The SAP Cryptographic Library. It is loaded in the same process, so I suspected it. nm showed it has no Kerberos code at all. It handles TLS and SSFS, not SNC with Kerberos.

How I tested the final fix

A fix that only survives one restart is not a fix. So I broke it on purpose: deleted the ticket with kdestroy, restarted a work process and watched it fail, let the cron job renew the ticket, restarted again and watched it recover. Then a full system restart. All good, and the same fix worked on a second system.

Conclusion and what is next

Read the trace for where it stopped, clear the simple errors, compare with a working system, and prove the theory with a command, not a guess. Most of my time went into the dead ends, and each one ruled something out.

Part 4 covers the second problem in detail: why SAP had a keytab but no ticket, what KCM and a file cache are, and the cron job that keeps the ticket fresh. I will add the link here once it is published. Follow me here on SAP Community to get notified, and tell me in the comments which check you start with when SNC breaks.

entry.title: SNC with Kerberos after migration, Part 4: "Initiating Credentials not available"
entry.content:
Introduction

About this series. After a data center migration to RHEL 9 and an Oracle 19c client, our SAP ABAP system would not start once SNC with Kerberos was switched on. Behind that one symptom were two separate problems.

  • Overview: the whole story and both fixes in short
  • Part 1: how SNC with Kerberos logs you into SAP without a password
  • Part 2: why the Oracle 19c client crashed the work process, and LD_PRELOAD
  • Part 3: how I proved it, and the dead ends
  • Part 4 (this post): "Initiating Credentials not available": keytab, ticket and credential cache
  • Part 5: runbook and cheat sheet

Part 2 fixed the crash. This post covers what came right after: SNC got one step further and stopped again, this time with a credentials error.

The error

SncInit(): found  snc/identity/as=p:<host>$@<REALM>
SncInit(): Accepting  Cred: "krb5" (0x0002) ok, lifetime=Indefinite
*** ERROR => SncPExportGSSName()==SNCERR_GSSAPI
FATAL SNCERR -- Initiating Credentials: "krb5" (0x0002) not available!
<<- SncInit()==SNCERR_GSSAPI    sec_avail = "false"

One line says OK, the next says not available. To read that, you need to know that SNC checks two different things when it starts.

Accepting and initiating: two different credentials

Accepting means: can SAP check the Kerberos tickets that users send in? For that, SAP only needs its own secret key, which is stored in the keytab (/etc/krb5.keytab). No contact with Active Directory is needed, which is why the trace says "lifetime=Indefinite". This was fine.

Initiating means: can SAP prove its own identity to others? For that, SAP needs a TGT, a ticket from Active Directory, sitting in a credential cache. That was missing.

Analogy: the keytab is the key to your own front door. You can always use it to let people in. The TGT is a day pass from the security desk that lets you walk into other buildings. It expires, and you have to collect it first. SAP had the key but no day pass, and SNC will not start without both.

Part 1 walks through this with a full login example.

Why there was no ticket

Two things came together.

Nobody was getting a ticket for the server. A keytab sits on disk and does nothing on its own. Someone has to run kinit with it to collect a TGT. On our system, nothing did that for the SAP user.

The wallet had moved. The credential cache is where tickets are kept after kinit, like a wallet. On RHEL 8 and 9 the default wallet is KCM, held inside the SSSD service. On the old SLES system it was a plain file. The SAP work processes are started by sapstartsrv, not by your terminal, so a ticket you can see in your own shell is not guaranteed to be in the wallet those processes read.

To be honest about it: my logs show that a file cache solved it. They do not show exactly why KCM did not. What I can say is that a file cache gives every SAP process, and the job that renews the ticket, one fixed place to look.

The fix

1. Give SAP one fixed wallet. In the profile of the <sid>adm user:

export KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/krb5cc_<SID>

2. Put a ticket in it, using the keytab instead of a password. As <sid>adm:

kdestroy
kinit -k -t /etc/krb5.keytab '<host>$'
klist        # should show krbtgt/<REALM>@<REALM> with an expiry time

The principal must match snc/identity/as, here the server's Active Directory computer account <host>$.

3. Restart SAP completely, so sapstartsrv and the work processes start with the new KRB5CCNAME. Environment variables are only read when a process starts.

stopsap all
lsnrctl start
startsap all

4. Keep the ticket fresh. A TGT from Active Directory lasts about 10 hours. A small cron job for <sid>adm runs the same kinit every few minutes. Cron does not read the user profile, so the cache path goes into the cron line itself, for example:

*/5 * * * * KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/krb5cc_<SID> /usr/bin/kinit -k -t /etc/krb5.keytab '<host>$'

Every five minutes is more than needed, but it is harmless and means a lost ticket comes back quickly.

How I tested it

  • Checked with klist that a new ticket appeared after each cron run.
  • Restarted work processes: they started and went back to waiting.
  • Stopped cron, deleted the ticket with kdestroy, restarted a work process: it failed SNC init, as expected.
  • Started cron again, waited for the next run, restarted the work process: it came up fine.
  • Full system restart: OK. The same fix worked on a second system.

Things to keep in mind

  • <sid>adm must be able to read the keytab. By default it is readable by root only.
  • If the cron job stops, running work processes keep working. Only work processes that start after the ticket expires will fail.
  • Kerberos is strict about time. If the server clock and the domain controller differ by more than a few minutes, kinit fails.

Conclusion and what is next

"Accepting OK, initiating not available" means the keytab is fine but SAP has no ticket of its own in the place it looks. Give it one fixed file cache, fill it with kinit from the keytab, and renew it with cron.

Part 5 brings everything from this series onto one page: the final configuration, a checklist after every restart, and an "error, cause, fix" table. I will add the link here once it is published. Follow me here on SAP Community to get notified, and tell me in the comments how you keep the SAP server's Kerberos ticket fresh on your systems.

entry.title: Before the First Prompt: How SAP Engineers Trust Before Agents Are Ever Invoked
entry.content:
As enterprise AI evolves from conversational assistants to agentic systems capable of retrieving enterprise information, invoking tools, and initiating business workflows, the security challenge extends beyond protecting models and prompts. It requires governing the identities, permissions, data flows, integrations, and actions that connect AI to enterprise systems.

Trust must be engineered through clearly defined security boundaries, enforceable authorization controls, data protection measures, and accountable execution paths.

The SAP Business AI Platform is architected with exactly this in mind.

The SAP Agentic AI Ecosystem

This is the first blog in a three-part series on the security and governance of the SAP Agentic AI ecosystem. This post covers the trust foundation: how SAP builds and validates agents before they reach your landscape, how they are provisioned, and how identity, authorization, and data isolation are enforced. Part two “ Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work”  covers the practitioner layer — using SAP agents, building custom extensions, and bridging third-party AI systems. Part three “The Agentic Glass Box: Observability and Governance at Enterprise Scale”concludes the series with the governance and observability architecture that gives enterprise teams the visibility and control to run AI at scale with confidence.

This post examines the first layer of that architecture — the controls SAP puts in place before a user sends a single message. It covers how security responsibilities are distributed across the agent supply chain, the provisioning model, and the identity and data isolation infrastructure; where those controls are enforced; and what enterprise IT leaders and CISOs should understand about the trust boundaries that govern agentic AI in SAP.

How SAP Ensures Agents Are Secure and Trustworthy Before You Provision Them

Every agent that appears in your SAP product catalog has passed through a structured security and governance program, built on a rigorous Secure Software Development and Operations Lifecycle, before it ever reaches your landscape. This program is built around the principle that trust must be earned through verifiable processes.

The foundation is controlled ownership and traceability. Each agent is formally registered within SAP with a defined owner, a declared scope, and a stable identity. It goes through multi-team review before it is eligible for customer deployment, and a complete Software Bill of Materials is generated automatically — documenting every component and dependency in the agent, giving a transparent view of what is running.

Security and governance are validated at every stage of development:

  • Every agent goes through a formal Ethics evaluation to verify fairness, transparency, human oversight (e.g., through human-in-the-loop) and alignment with global data privacy laws before development begins.
  • Agents go through a rigorous threat evaluation exercise performed to identify and mitigate risks during the design phase.
  • Code security is checked through mandatory automated scans covering application vulnerabilities, exposed credentials, and known weaknesses in third-party libraries, before the agent advances toward production
  • Authorization is managed as policy - agent-to-API permissions (e.g. read on a specific S/4 API resource) are assigned automatically during tenant mapping and provisioned as authorization policies in SAP Cloud Identity Services.
  • Audit logging is non-negotiable — every agent must implement security event logging.
  • All AI model interactions are routed through SAP AI Core — ensuring data residency, content filtering, and prompt injection protection can be enforced consistently, depending on the risk profile of the Agent.

Deployment follows a controlled, staged release process across development, test, and pre-production environments. Each step toward production requires an explicit human decision — there is no automated approval path from development to your landscape. The artifact that was validated in testing is the exact same artifact that reaches production; nothing is rebuilt or changed along the way.

Finally, every agent undergoes a formal security review before production release. The shared infrastructure SAP manages on your behalf — identity, network security, tenant isolation, geo-blocking — is covered automatically. The security review validates the agent's own logic, access controls, and AI-specific risks on top of the baseline.

By the time you see an agent in your SAP product catalog, it carries a documented chain of custody: who built it, what it contains, what security gates it passed, and what authorization model it enforces.

SAP for Me: Your Unified Hub for Subscription and Automated Provisioning

The lifecycle of an enterprise agent is governed by SAP for Me, which serves as the centralized control plane for provisioning and subscription management. This interface streamlines the deployment of Joule components, replacing complex manual BTP formations with a guided "Start Provisioning" workflow.

  • Governed Activation & Licensing: Customers activate specific agent scenarios (e.g., Finance Assistant, HR Service Desk) directly through SAP for Me. Access is strictly gated by valid subscription licenses (such as Joule-based or Early Adopter Care SKUs) and landscape prerequisites (e.g., connected S/4HANA or SuccessFactors systems). This ensures that only licensed, technically compatible agents are deployed within the enterprise topology.
  • Managed Orchestration & Trust: Under the SAP Managed Joule model, SAP assumes responsibility for the underlying infrastructure, including the Agent Gateway Formation. This mandatory formation establishes the secure, Service Provider Integration Interface (SPII) - based trust foundation (via IAS-backed destinations and token exchange) required for agent-to-agent communication. SAP manages the continuous updates, patching, and operational health of this global trust infrastructure, freeing customers from managing core AI runtime security.
  • Principal Propagation & Boundary Enforcement: Activation initiates the automated creation of service formations within the designated BTP subaccount. Security boundaries are enforced through principal propagation, where the Agent Gateway ensures that agent actions strictly respect the end-user's existing roles and identity context. This guarantees that agents operate only on data accessible to the user, preventing cross-tenant leakage or privilege escalation across integrated solutions.

 Example: Enabling Joule and AI Features in SAP SuccessFactors

By automating the technical "plumbing" in the background, SAP4Me allows you to maintain control over your high-level service settings while simplifying the onboarding experience.

The Identity & Authorization Framework (IAM) for SAP Agentic AI

 SAP Joule utilizes a robust governance model where AI agents are treated as first-class citizens—distinct service principals with their own boundaries and permissions. This architecture is built on SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS), which serves as the trust anchor and sole token issuer for agent identities.

To understand how this secures your data, we must look at the four distinct validation layers defined in the architecture:

 1. End user Authentication

End-users authenticate via standard enterprise protocols (OIDC/SAML) through SAP Cloud Identity Services. 

2. Validating User-to-Agent Access (Connectivity Governance)

The First Line of Defence. Before an agent even begins to work, the system must answer: "Is this user allowed to talk to this specific agent?"

  • How it works: When a user invokes Joule, the request is routed through the Agent Gateway which acts as the enforced single entry point for connectivity.
  • The Mechanism: Two layers work together
    • System connectivity is established through a UCL (Unified Customer Landscape) formation, which onboards the tenants/systems and wires up the trust (IAS App2App dependencies) between them. If that connection hasn't been formed, the caller can't even obtain a valid token to reach the agent.
    • User authorization is then checked against AMS (Authorization Management Service) policies — this is the per-user "is this user permitted to invoke this agent?" decision. (Agent and tool metadata itself lives in BTP, which is what the Gateway resolves the target against.).

A caller that is not connected and authorized is rejected before reaching the agent.

 3. Validating Agent-to-Tool Access (Orchestration Governance)

The Handshake. Once a user connects to an agent, the system must answer: "Is this agent allowed to use this tool?"

  • How it works: The Agent Gateway acts as a transparent proxy in front of tools and other agents. When an agent needs to execute a task, it presents its own IAS-issued, certificate-bound token; the Gateway performs the token exchange and injects the right credentials toward the target service.
  • The Mechanism: The Agent Gateway enforces authorization policies via AMS, checking whether a specific agent is allowed to call a specific tool (this is done with IAS token validation, mTLS, and tenant-mapping checks). This keeps every agent inside its defined scope — e.g., an HR agent can reach its HR systems but can't invoke a Finance tool it was never granted.

4. Validating Data Access (Functional Authorization)

The Final Security Layer. Finally, the system must answer: "Is this request allowed to see/read/write this specific data?"

  • How it works: The target application (e.g., SAP S/4HANA) enforces standard SAP Cloud Application authorization.
  • The Mechanism: This relies on established SAP concepts of Roles, Roles Catalogs, and Scopes. The agent's token includes the context of the original user. Therefore, the target application ensures that the action is only performed if the human user has permission to see that data (Row-Level Security).

This multi-layered approach ensures that governance is not a single point of failure. The system fails early: if the user lacks connectivity, the agent is never called; if the agent lacks functional authorization, the data is never touched.

 Data Segregation & Isolation

 A core tenet of Joule security is strict tenant isolation at every layer of the stack:

Your business data remains strictly isolated within your specific Line of Business applications, governed by the proven, multi-tenant security architecture already established in the backend systems. Access to this data is governed by the existing application logic, ensuring that even AI interaction is strictly constrained by functional or business rules supported by authorization.

 Metadata within the SAP Knowledge Graph and data in SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine is strictly partitioned per Tenant. Joule leverages the SAP BTP multi-tenancy infrastructure to ensure that every query is bound to a specific tenant context. This ensures that there is no cross-tenant data leakage or overlap.

Joule utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to access enterprise data through the Generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core. Crucially, this process is automated and governed by strict multi-tenant isolation:

  • Automated Onboarding: You do not manually manage files or keys. Instead, you define "Grounding Sources" in the Generative AI Hub, pointing it to your backend systems (e.g., S/4HANA CDS Views, SAP Build Work Zone) via generic secrets. The platform automatically extracts metadata and ingests the content securely.
  • Tenant-Safe Vectorization: For unstructured data like PDFs or documents, the system processes the text and converts it into numerical vectors (embeddings). These are stored in the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine, where every piece of data is partitioned by your unique tenant identifier.
  • Architectural Isolation: Data separation is enforced at the infrastructure level through the platform's multi-tenancy model, which scopes every query to the caller's tenant context. This ensures that Joule can never retrieve or process data from another tenant.

Your prompts to Joule and the retrieved or processed data in Joule Work is not shared with third-party LLM providers for the purpose of training or improving their models. Your data is only sent to the LLM provider for processing and is not stored or otherwise retained by the LLM providers.

 

To Be Continued…

The controls described here are what make agentic AI deployable with confidence. But a secure foundation only matters if what you build on top of it holds up. Part two “ Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work”  covers exactly that.

entry.title: The Agentic Glass Box: Observability and Governance at Enterprise Scale
entry.content:
Knowing that an agent was built securely and knowing that it is behaving securely right now are two different things. The trust foundation that Part one described — vetted supply chains, governed provisioning, enforced identity — is a starting point, not a guarantee. Agents evolve. Configurations change. New integrations are added. The ecosystem grows. And as it grows, the need for visibility becomes not a nice-to-have but a hard governance requirement.

Enterprise AI cannot operate as a black box. Not for regulators. Not for auditors. Not for the IT and security teams responsible for what happens when an agent makes the wrong call at scale. The answer is a glass box approach: every agent action observable, every identity traceable, every data access auditable — not eventually, but by design, from the moment an agent is deployed.

This is the third and final post in the series. Part one ”Before the First Prompt: How SAP Engineers Trust Before Agents Are Ever Invoked” built the trust foundation. Part two “ Use Existing Agents, Build New Ones, Connect to Others — All Securely with SAP Joule Work”  covered using, extending, and connecting agents. This post closes the loop — the governance and observability layer that gives enterprise teams real-time visibility, cross-platform control, and compliance-grade audit trails across the entire Joule Work ecosystem.

It covers three areas: how Joule Work's security model adapts across Web, Mobile, and Desktop; how the SAP AI Agent Hub in SAP LeanIX acts as a vendor-agnostic command centre for governing every AI asset in your landscape; and how the monitoring and audit architecture — built on OpenTelemetry, the SAP Audit Log Service, and integrated with Cloud ALM and Signavio — delivers the traceability enterprise governance demands.

 Governance Across Modalities

Joule adapts its security posture to the device context: Web, Mobile, and Desktop.

Joule Work Web

Joule Work Web is the core AI workspace running in the browser with a platform-first security model focused on tenant isolation, identity-bound access, and governed agent execution.

  • Identity: Access is gated by SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) Identity Authentication Service (IAS) by assigning users to the joule_end_user group.
  • Session Management: Uses token-based session management with short expiration times.
  • Network Security: All communication occurs over secure TLS.
  • Data access: Joule responses only surface data the authenticated user is already authorized to see
  • Tenant-level data isolation : Customer data stays within the customer's own SAP tenancy; no customer data is stored within Joule itself

Joule Work Mobile App

Joule Work Mobile brings Joule to the enterprise edge — iOS, Android, and wearables — with a security model anchored in device governance, MDM-enforced access policies, and full data erasure on offboarding

  • SSO via short-lived tokens, with SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) as the primary IdP — supports proxy to corporate IdPs (e.g. Microsoft Entra ID)
  • Configurable Remember Me session cookies when IAS is active
  • MDM integration enables automated onboarding, conditional access, and app protection policies
  • Remote wipe and inactivity-based auto-deregistration remove access and data on lost or inactive devices
  • Local data encrypted with AES-256 (iOS additionally uses Keychain); all traffic over HTTPS
  • Sign-out permanently removes all personal data and configurations from the device
  • Access to security settings, feature flags, and user management is gated by a dedicated MobileAdmin BTP Role Collection
  • Enterprise app distribution requires signed builds (Apple certificates/provisioning profiles); admin-configurable support log uploads for audit and troubleshooting

Refer: Joule Work Mobile App – Administration Guide

Joule Work Desktop

Joule Work Desktop extends AI capabilities to local files (PDFs, Code, Office docs) with a unique security model focused on data privacy:

  • Users must be explicitly assigned — no self-service enrolment. Authentication and Authorizations is managed by SAP IAS
  • User conversations remain locally stored on user device, user can delete at any time.
  • The Desktop extension acts as a sandboxed process. It cannot access the operating system's clipboard or other application memory without specific, user-initiated actions.
  • Governance of which MCPs the user can use, happens via the Admin UI. In the Admin UI, customer admins can define allow/blocklists for certain MCPs. These settings are fetched by the client and enforced on client side. User can only enable those MCP servers on the client which are allowed.

 

Vendor-agnostic command center - SAP AI Agent Hub

 

SAP AI Agent Hub: Your command center for AI governance

AI Agent Hub works in conjecture with already existing SAP products (Ex: Cloud ALM, Signavio, SuccessFactors) to enhance the experience of building an agent, monitoring of the process and agent health and workforce impact. We will discuss these capabilities below.

 

Architecture Decisions Inventory

 By integrating SAP LeanIX’s context-rich enterprise architecture inventory with the AI Agent Hub, organizations embed governance directly into the agent development lifecycle. The Architecture Decisions view captures foundational technical and policy choices (e.g., LLM framework selection, PII data handling strategies, initial scaling limits) and automatically surfaces these guardrails during agent creation. This ensures new agents are aligned with established architectural standards from day one rather than requiring retrospective remediation.

Real-Time Landscape Discovery & Dependency Mapping

During development, the integrated MCP server continuously queries the live LeanIX landscape to perform automated capability mapping and dependency analysis. As the agent builder progresses through business understanding, fit-gap assessment, and process design, it automatically:

  • Identifies relevant existing agents (e.g., Invoice Mapper Agent)
  • Surfaces supporting applications & data sources (e.g., S/4HANA Private Cloud, Oracle, custom SAP systems)
  • Maps cross-system dependencies and process touchpoints

This eliminates manual landscape research and ensures agents are grounded in the actual enterprise architecture, preventing duplicate investments and unplanned integration risks.

 

AI Agent Discovery Inbox

SAP AI Agent Hub — a capability within SAP LeanIX — has the AI Agent Discovery Inbox which provides centralized visibility into all AI artifacts across the enterprise—agents, MCP servers, and LLM instances—regardless of origin or vendor. Integrated usage analytics (activation history, session volume, trend patterns) enable governance teams to prioritize high-impact interventions. Discovered assets enter a unified workflow for rapid assessment, classification, and inventory onboarding.

 

Verification Workflow & Compliance Enforcement

Unlike traditional platforms that treat agents as isolated IT components, SAP AI Agent Hub maps each agent as a first-class enterprise architecture artifact. Every agent is explicitly linked to:

  • The business capability it enables
  • Downstream applications and data flows it depends on
  • The value stream/processes it participates in

The Verification Workflow subject all inventory entries to structured assessment against organizational risk criteria, compliance mandates, and architecture standards. Successful verification generates a formal audit trail capturing approval authority, ownership, operational scope, and dependency impact. Only verified agents are permitted in production, effectively closing the approve-to-run gap and standardizing governance expectations across development teams.

 

Agent Operation Overview

Agent Mining in SAP Signavio applies process mining algorithms to agent execution traces, reconstructing how agents actually behave in production. It produces a discovered execution model showing every path taken, path frequency, and deviations from the intended design — going beyond session-level observability to surface the full range of execution variants, including edge cases.

Agent Performance Deep Drive

The view above in SAP Signavio Agent Mining translates the mined execution model into prioritized optimization opportunities, functioning as a closed-loop business-outcome feedback mechanism. By connecting behavioral patterns directly to measurable KPIs, it quantifies return on investment and surfaces actionable insights. When agents follow incorrect execution paths at high frequency, it signals a systematic misalignment between agent design and business intent—not merely an isolated failure. Optimization potential is evaluated not only on technical metrics but on actual process outcomes: is the workflow the agent was deployed to improve actually performing better? This closes the gap between agent deployment and tangible value realization, enabling organizations to focus efforts on their most effective agents—answering the ROI and performance questions that leadership increasingly demands but few can currently provide.

 

AI Agent Monitoring in SAP Cloud ALM provides two levels of visibility into agent health and behaviour across the enterprise.

Deep Dive View

Session-Level Visibility (Deep Dive): Traces a single execution of the agent in detail—covering latency, token usage, and tool invocation flows. By utilizing underlying OpenTelemetry traces, engineers can reproduce issues, inspect reasoning steps, and understand exactly how the agent interacted with backend systems like S/4HANA. Every session is logged to ensure compliance-grade auditability.

High-Level View

Portfolio-Level Overview (High-Level): Displays the aggregate health of an agent across the environment using real-time dashboards. Key metrics such as Goal Completion Rate and Total Call Accuracy trend over time, allowing teams to quickly distinguish between isolated incidents and systemic issues. If an anomaly is detected, the dashboard provides a root-cause breakdown of the risk category (e.g., usage spikes or accuracy drops), enabling rapid response and data-driven governance decisions.

 

SAP SucessFactors Integration

SAP SuccessFactors helps you understand how your agent deployment strategy is reshaping your workforce. Each agent is mapped to the business units and roles it affects, giving HR and business leaders visibility into which skills are impacted, which teams are using agents, and how the workforce is changing as AI deployment scales.

Together, these integrations span the full agent governance lifecycle. SAP LeanIX grounds every agent in the enterprise architecture — ensuring it is aligned to established standards. SAP AI Agent Hub discovers the agents, the agents can be verified and enabled for production. SAP Signavio reveals how agents actually behave once deployed, surfacing deviations from intended design and connecting execution patterns to business outcomes. SAP Cloud ALM provides the operational layer — real-time health monitoring at both the session and portfolio level, with the depth engineers need to investigate and the breadth leadership needs to govern. SAP SuccessFactors closes the loop on the human side, mapping agent deployment to workforce and organizations. 

Observability and Compliance

Trust requires visibility. Joule provides a "Glass Box" architecture for enterprise monitoring:

  • Observability (OpenTelemetry): Agent runtimes are instrumented with OpenTelemetry — the standard SAP has adopted for logs, metrics, and traces — and Joule Studio's Traces & Explainability surface lets users inspect agent execution traces for transparency and debugging.
  • Audit logging (SAP Audit Log Service): Security-relevant events generated by agents and their interactions — such as authentications, authorization/validation errors, and unauthenticated access attempts — are recorded through the SAP Audit Log Service (the BTP audit log offering)
  • SIEM integration: Audit log events are forwarded from the SAP Audit Log Service to enterprise SIEM systems for further security analysis.
  • Content safety: Inputs and outputs can pass through AI Core Orchestration Service's content filtering, they scan for and block non-compliant content.
  • Runtime containment (NVIDIA OpenShell): SAP's collaboration with NVIDIA embeds OpenShell into the Joule Studio runtime, providing isolated execution boundaries, network and filesystem policy enforcement, and runtime-level auditability — ensuring agent actions are governed and inspectable at the environment level, independent of the model or application code.

Summary

This series has traced the governance challenge of enterprise agentic AI from its origin to its resolution. Part one established the trust foundation before agents are ever invoked — supply chain controls, provisioning governance, and identity architecture that ensure every agent starts from a verified baseline. Part two showed how that foundation holds under the pressure of real work: users engaging through Conversations and Spaces, developers extending the platform via Joule Studio and BYOA paths, and the enterprise bridging its SAP systems to third-party AI ecosystems — all within a "one governed door" architecture enforced by the Agent Gateway. This post closed the loop, demonstrating how Joule's security model adapts across Web, Mobile, and Desktop modalities; how the SAP AI Agent Hub provides a vendor-agnostic command center that maps every AI asset back to the business processes and risk criteria it touches; and how observability — through OpenTelemetry, the SAP Audit Log Service, SIEM integration, and NVIDIA OpenShell's runtime containment — transforms Joule Work into a glass box.

Note: this architecture is evolving — capabilities, integrations, and controls described here will continue to develop as the platform matures.

entry.title: SNC with Kerberos after migration, Part 5: runbook and cheat sheet
entry.content:
Introduction

About this series. After a data center migration to RHEL 9 and an Oracle 19c client, our SAP ABAP system would not start once SNC with Kerberos was switched on. Behind that one symptom were two separate problems.

  • Overview: the whole story and both fixes in short
  • Part 1: how SNC with Kerberos logs you into SAP without a password
  • Part 2: why the Oracle 19c client crashed the work process, and LD_PRELOAD
  • Part 3: how I proved it, and the dead ends
  • Part 4: "Initiating Credentials not available": keytab, ticket and credential cache
  • Part 5 (this post): runbook and cheat sheet

This last part is the one to bookmark. No story, just everything from the series on one page: the final configuration, what to check after a restart, and what to do when a specific error shows up.

Final configuration

Instance profile

snc/enable              = 1
snc/gssapi_lib          = /usr/lib64/libgssapi_krb5.so
snc/identity/as         = p:<host>$@<REALM>
snc/data_protection/min = 2
snc/data_protection/max = 3
snc/data_protection/use = 3

Profile of the <sid>adm user

export LD_PRELOAD=/lib64/libgssapi_krb5.so.2:/lib64/libkrb5.so.3:/lib64/libk5crypto.so.3:/lib64/libkrb5support.so.0
export KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/krb5cc_<SID>

Crontab of <sid>adm (example)

*/5 * * * * KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/krb5cc_<SID> /usr/bin/kinit -k -t /etc/krb5.keytab '<host>$'

Start sequence

kdestroy
kinit -k -t /etc/krb5.keytab '<host>$'
klist
stopsap all
lsnrctl start
startsap all

Checklist after every restart or OS patch

  1. As <sid>adm, echo $LD_PRELOAD and echo $KRB5CCNAME both show the values above.
  2. The four preloaded files still exist under /lib64 with the same names.
  3. klist shows a valid krbtgt ticket in the file cache, not expired.
  4. crontab -l still has the renewal job.
  5. The latest dev_w trace shows "dynamically loaded as GSS-API v2 library", "Accepting Cred ... ok", and no "Initiating Credentials not available".
  6. All work processes are running in SM50, and an SNC logon from SAP GUI works.

Error, cause, fix

What you see Most likely cause What to do

What you seeMost likely causeWhat to do
dlopen FAILED, No such file or directory, SNCERR_INITsnc/gssapi_lib points to a library that does not exist (for example an old Quest path)Point it to /usr/lib64/libgssapi_krb5.so
SIGABRT, stack shows krb5int functions inside libclntsh.soOracle client's copy of Kerberos is called instead of MIT KerberosSet LD_PRELOAD as above, full restart (Part 2)
Accepting ok, Initiating Credentials not availableNo valid ticket in the cache SAP readsCheck KRB5CCNAME, kinit with the keytab, check cron (Part 4)
kinit: Client not found in Kerberos databaseWrong principal name, or the computer account was reset in ADUse <host>$, check the keytab with klist -k
kinit: Permission denied on the keytab<sid>adm cannot read /etc/krb5.keytabAdjust permissions or use a copy readable by <sid>adm
kinit: Clock skew too greatServer time differs from the domain controllerFix time sync (chrony or NTP)
SAP starts, but SSO logon failsSNC name in SAP Logon differs from snc/identity/as, or no SNC name in SU01Align the names, maintain the SNC tab in SU01

Three things I would tell my past self

  • After a migration, check every library path in the SNC parameters before anything else.
  • If Kerberos functions show up inside the Oracle client in a crash stack, it is a library clash, not an SNC setting.
  • A keytab is not a ticket. SAP needs both, and the ticket must be renewed.

Conclusion

That closes the series. One symptom, two problems, and two fixes that are each only a few lines long. Finding them took much longer than applying them, which is why I wrote it all down.

Thank you for following along. If this runbook saves you a few hours, or if you solved the same problem in a different way, tell me in the comments. Follow me here on SAP Community for the next series.

entry.title: Configuring SSL Encryption Between SAP ABAP Application Servers and SAP HANA
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog documents the steps required to configure SSL/TLS encryption between SAP ABAP application servers and an SAP HANA database, using a certificate signed by an external Certificate Authority (CA). This is a common requirement in enterprise migrations and security hardening projects where the default SAP-generated certificates are replaced with organisation-specific ones.

The configuration covered here implements TLS — the HANA database server authenticates itself to the ABAP application layer. sapcli.pse on each ABAP node serves as the trust store, allowing the ABAP kernel to verify HANA's certificate during the TLS handshake. This guide assumes you are working on a Linux-based SAP system with SAP CommonCryptoLib installed.

Prerequisites

  • Database certificate (.pfx format) signed by an external CA, plus the corresponding root certificate
  • Certificate password
  • Access to the HANA database server at OS level (sidadm or equivalent)
  • Access to all ABAP application server nodes at OS level
  • A valid HANA userstore key configured for hdbsql commands
  • Planned downtime or maintenance window — the ABAP application must be stopped during parts of this procedure
  • Existing SAPSSLS.pse backed up before making any changes

Overview

The procedure creates two sets of PSE (Personal Security Environment) files:

  1. SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA server — the HANA database server's SSL identity, built from the externally signed certificate. This is what HANA presents to the ABAP layer during the TLS handshake.

  2. sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse on each ABAP application server — these are placed in the sec directory of each ABAP node. They act as the trust store on the ABAP side, containing the CA certificate chain that the ABAP kernel uses to verify HANA's certificate. The sslKeyStore reference in the profile parameter also points to sapcli.pse, but since sslclientpki is off on HANA, the client certificate is never requested.

Step 1 — Upload Certificates to the HANA Server

  1. Log on to the HANA database server at OS level as sidadm
  2. Upload the database certificate (db_cert.pfx), the root certificate (root.cer) (and any intermediate certificates) to the sec directory on the HANA server:
/usr/sap/<SID>/SYS/global/security/rsecssls/

Note: The exact sec directory path may vary. Confirm the location using the SECUDIR environment variable.

  1. Before making any changes, back up the existing SAPSSLS.pse:
cp SAPSSLS.pse SAPSSLS.pse.bak

Step 2 — Create SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA Server

Run the following command to create a new SAPSSLS.pse from the externally signed certificate. This becomes the HANA server's SSL identity:

sapgenpse import_p12 -r root.cer -p SAPSSLS.pse <db_cert.pfx>
  • Enter the certificate password when prompted
  • When asked for a PIN, you have the option to set one or leave it empty. From a security perspective, setting a PIN is recommended as it adds an additional layer of protection to the PSE file. If a PIN is set, ensure it is stored securely as it will be required for any future PSE operations

SAPSSLS.pse should now be created successfully.

Step 3 — Create the Client PSE Files for ABAP Application Servers

sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse can be created directly from SAPSSLS.pse:

cp SAPSSLS.pse sapcli.pse
cp SAPSSLS.pse sapsrv.pse

Copy both files to the sec directory on every ABAP application server node (CS/CI and all additional application servers):

/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/

Step 4 — Disable sslclientpki on HANA

Important: Shut down the ABAP application layer before executing this step.

This parameter controls whether HANA enforces client PKI certificate authentication. Setting it to off enables one-way TLS (server authentication only), which is the configuration used here.

Run the following hdbsql command from the HANA server:

hdbsql -U <USERSTORE_KEY> "ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') SET ('communication', 'sslclientpki') = 'off' WITH RECONFIGURE;"

The WITH RECONFIGURE clause applies the change immediately without requiring a HANA restart.

PRD Systems: This parameter must also be disabled on the secondary/DR HANA node. This can be done via SAP HANA Studio — apply the change on both the primary and DR secondary database nodes.

Step 5 — Configure the ABAP Default Profile

The dbs/hdb/connect_property parameter must be added to the ABAP default profile (DEFAULT.PFL) to instruct the ABAP kernel to use SSL when connecting to HANA. This parameter applies to all application server instances.

Add the following parameter (adapt values to your system):

dbs/hdb/connect_property = ENCRYPT=TRUE,sslCryptoProvider=commoncrypto,sslKeyStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslTrustStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslHostNameInCertificate=<hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com>

Key values to adapt:

  • <SID> — your system ID
  • <instance_dir> — the instance directory of each application server (e.g. D00, D01)
  • <hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com> — the fully qualified hostname as it appears in the HANA certificate's CN/SAN field

Note: The sslHostNameInCertificate value must match exactly what is embedded in the HANA server certificate, otherwise the SSL handshake will fail.

Step 6 — Restart the Application and Validate

Start the ABAP application layer. Once all instances are up, perform the following validation steps.

Validation 1 — Check encrypted connections via SQL

Log on to the system and navigate to transaction DB02 → SQL Editor. Run the following statement, replacing <SCHEMA> with the correct database schema name:

SELECT IS_ENCRYPTED, SSL_VERSION, CLIENT_HOST
FROM SYS.M_CONNECTIONS
WHERE USER_NAME = '<SCHEMA>'
AND IS_ENCRYPTED = 'TRUE';

All active connections for the schema should return TRUE in the IS_ENCRYPTED column. If any sessions return FALSE, review the profile parameter and PSE file placement.

Validation 2 — R3trans connectivity check

Run the following from the OS level on each application server to confirm no transport-layer issues:

R3trans -d

Review the trans.log output — a clean run with no errors confirms successful connectivity between the ABAP application layer and HANA over SSL.

Summary

At this point, SSL encryption between the SAP ABAP application servers and SAP HANA is active using an externally signed CA certificate. The HANA server authenticates to the application layer via SAPSSLS.pse, while each ABAP node uses sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse as its trust store for verifying HANA's identity.

This guide was produced by the IT Planning and Software Logistics team, SAP Ireland, based on field experience from enterprise RISE migration projects.

entry.title: Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model on SAP BTP: Who Owns What?
entry.content:
When you move workloads to SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), one of the first governance questions you need to answer is deceptively simple: who is responsible for what?

It's a question that often goes unanswered until something goes wrong - a security incident, a compliance gap, an outage that exposes unclear ownership. The SAP BTP Admin Guide addresses this head-on with a clearly defined Shared Responsibility Model and understanding it is foundational to operating on the platform safely and effectively.

It's Not a Two-Party Model - It's Three

Most teams think of shared responsibility as a binary: SAP handles the platform; we handle our apps. But SAP BTP involves three distinct parties:

 

What SAP Is Responsible For

As the service provider, SAP is responsible for the following areas:

  • Global Accounts and Entitlements Provisioning

SAP creates your global account and assigns the necessary entitlements so you can start using SAP BTP. During this provisioning process, SAP grants initial global account administrator rights to your designated administrator.

  • Runtimes and Services Management

SAP manages and operates the core BTP services and runtimes - including Cloud Foundry, SAP Integration Suite, and SAP Build - and keeps them updated and secure. Depending on the runtime you use, you share responsibility differently: Kyma gives you full cluster access except the SAP-managed Kyma-system namespace, while the ABAP environment lets you manage select aspects via the Landscape Portal.

 

What You Are Responsible For

As an SAP BTP customer, you’re responsible for the following areas:

  • Change Management and Operations

You establish and run effective change management processes for your applications and integrations. If you use open-source software, you must keep it updated and include vulnerability scanning in your development process.

  • Customer Data and Content

You are responsible for your data and content, which includes ensuring data privacy.

  • Application Development and Integration

You develop and operate your applications on SAP BTP. This includes creating, deploying, and integrating them with other systems.

  • Account and Environment Management

You manage your account structure, which includes organizing directories, subaccounts, and service instances. You define an account strategy based on your organization's requirements, create and configure subaccounts for your development projects, and allocate resources and services as needed.

  • Authorization and Identity Management

You manage users and assign authorizations according to your organizational and project needs. To meet these needs, use the authorization and identity management tools that SAP provides.

 

The Shared Zones: Where Collaboration Is Essential

You and SAP share responsibility for the following key areas:

  • Observability

SAP handles platform-level monitoring for all BTP services - covering health checks, troubleshooting, housekeeping, and incident management. As a customer, you're expected to leverage BTP's built-in monitoring tools, add your own checks where needed, and manage housekeeping for your own components. If an issue falls under SAP's responsibility, raise an incident through the standard SAP support process.

  • Security and Compliance

SAP treats security and compliance as a core priority on BTP. They adhere to strict industry standards across cybersecurity, operations, and privacy, and manage risks through comprehensive programs that cover cloud environments, physical facilities, events, and employees - ensuring your data is protected and regulatory requirements are met.

  • High Availability and Disaster Recovery

SAP guarantees high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR) for all SAP-managed BTP services through strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs), regular backups, and built-in disaster recovery mechanisms. However, customers also carry responsibility -particularly when deploying custom applications and extensions. This includes running a minimum of three instances where applicable and configuring SAP HANA Cloud with replicas to ensure resilience and for the overall HA/DR setup to work as intended.

 

Infrastructure Provider's Responsibilities

The infrastructure level is managed by either SAP or a hyperscaler, with SAP overseeing the relationship with hyperscalers. Even when using hyperscaler regions, SAP is responsible for managing this relationship. As a customer using SAP BTP, you don't have to interact directly with the hyperscalers.

The infrastructure providers operate the physical data centers that host SAP BTP regions. Their responsibilities include:

  • Set up and maintain the data centers, including servers, networking, and power supply.
  • Ensure physical and digital security to prevent unauthorized access.
  • Meet industry-grade standards for reliability and compliance.
  • Manage infrastructure operations, including software updates and patches.

 

Why This Model Matters in Practice

For Enterprise Architects and BTP administrators, the shared responsibility model is not just a governance document - it is an operational checklist. It drives decisions about:

  • Team structure: Who in your organization owns account governance? Who owns application security? Are those roles clearly defined and staffed?
  • Security controls: Are you applying SAP's security recommendations at the application and identity layer, or assuming the platform handles it all?
  • Compliance posture: Regulators will ask what you did to protect data - "SAP is responsible for the platform" will not cover application-layer gaps
  • Incident readiness: When something goes wrong, do you have the audit logs, monitoring, and runbooks to respond within your scope - or will you be scrambling to understand what you own?

 

📔Further Reading:

  • Shared Responsibility Model Between You and SAP — SAP BTP Admin Guide
  • SAP Trust Center
  • Resilience, High Availability, and Disaster Recovery

 

SAP's Customer Quality Check (CQC) services - the Security Optimization Service (SOS) and Transport Execution Analysis (TEA) - give customers a structured, expert-led way to fulfil their side of the shared responsibility model on SAP BTP. SOS surfaces misconfigured security settings across your BTP landscape with prioritized, actionable recommendations, while TEA identifies risks in how changes move through your environment. Together, they turn the abstract concept of shared responsibility into something measurable and manageable - available to customers on SAP Enterprise Support or Mission Critical Support.

  • SAP Community blog: Introducing Self-Service Booking in SAP for Me
  • Watch this short overview video
  • Explore the Services & Support FAQs
  • SAP Support Portal Continuous Quality Check & Improvement Services

 

🔗Stay connected 

Want to stay up to date on our services? Join our SAP Cloud ALM & Cross-Solution Topics community! 

🔔Stay tuned for my upcoming blogs based on Operating Model, SAP BTP Security Recommendations.
