entry.title: Stop Clicking, Start Scripting: Automate BTP Role Collection Mapping to IAS Groups via REST APIs
entry.content:
Introduction

Picture this: a customer is going live with a new SAP BTP landscape. Their IAS tenant already has user groups set up, their role collections are defined, and all that's left is connecting the two. Simple enough: in the BTP cockpit, navigate to Security → Trust Configuration → your IAS trust → Role Collection Mappings, and add one mapping at a time.

Now imagine doing that hundreds of times.

That was the reality for one of my customers. 130 role collections, each needing to be mapped to its corresponding IAS user group. At a conservative 3-4 minutes per mapping, finding the right collection, typing the group name exactly right, saving, repeat. You're looking at close to 8 hours of repetitive, error-prone cockpit work.

As a BTP consultant, I've seen this scenario play out more than once. And every time, the frustration is the same: the platform has everything you need, yet you're stuck doing something a machine should be doing for you.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service REST API to map BTP role collections to IAS user groups programmatically, saving hours of manual work, eliminating typo-induced errors, and giving you a reusable script you can run across every environment in your landscape.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • Subaccount Administrator role collection assigned to your user in the target BTP subaccount
  • A BTP subaccount with an IAS tenant configured as a custom identity provider
  • IAS user groups already created and populated with users
  • BTP CLI installed and configured
  • A REST client for testing: curl, Postman, or Bruno all work fine
  • Node.js (v18+) for the automation script (if you're creating a Node.js script like me)

 

Let's get scripting

Step 1 — Get API Credentials via the BTP CLI

To call the XSUAA REST API, you need a client credential pair. The cleanest way to get one is directly through the BTP CLI. No service instance or service key required.

btp login --sso
btp target --subaccount <SUBACCOUNT_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

Note:  This is the current recommended approach, replacing the deprecated apiaccess XSUAA service plan. If you come across older tutorials using "cf create-service xsuaa apiaccess" that approach still works but is being phased out.

The command returns a JSON object. Save these four values, you'll need all of them:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url (the token endpoint)
  • apiurl (the API base URL)

Step 2 — Get a Bearer Token

With the credentials in hand, request an OAuth token using the client credentials flow:

curl --request POST \
--url <url> \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data 'client_id=<clientid>' \
--data 'client_secret=<clientsecret>' \
--data 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
--data 'response_type=token'

Copy the access_token value from the response. You'll use it as a Bearer token in the next steps.

Step 3 — Check Existing Mappings (Optional but Recommended)

Before writing anything, it's worth checking what mappings already exist for your IAS identity provider. This gives you a baseline and avoids surprises:

curl --request GET \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

Where to find the IAS Origin Key: In your BTP subaccount, go to Security → Trust Configuration and click on your IAS trust entry. The Origin Key is shown in the detail panel. It typically looks like <something>.accounts.ondemand.com.

Step 4 — Create a Single Mapping

Now for the actual mapping call. Let's do one manually first to confirm everything works before running a bulk script:

curl --request POST \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>' \
--header 'content-type: application/json' \
--data '{
"attributeName": "Groups",
"attributeValue": "<IAS_Group_Name>",
"operator": "equals",
"roleCollectionName": "<BTP_Role_Collection_Name>"
}'

A few things to pay attention to:

  • attributeName must be exactly "Groups" with capital G, case-sensitive. This is the single most common mistake, and it fails without a helpful error message, so double-check this first.
  • attributeValue is the IAS group name, not the group ID.
  • roleCollectionName must match the role collection name exactly as it appears in the BTP cockpit.

A successful call returns HTTP 201 with the created mapping. To verify: go to BTP Cockpit → Security → Role Collections → open your role collection → User Groups tab. Your IAS group should now appear there.

Step 5 — Scale It Up: Automate with a Node.js Script

One mapping confirmed, now let's do all 130. The script below reads a list of mappings from a JSON file, fetches a token, and loops through each entry.

Project structure:

  • mappings.json – your list of group → role collection pairs
  • map-roles.mjs – the script
  • .env – credentials (never commit or publish this!)

.env

TOKEN_URL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
API_URL=https://api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
IAS_ORIGIN_KEY=<your-ias-origin-key>

mappings.json

[
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_ADMINS",
        "roleCollection": "Subaccount Administrator"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_DEVELOPERS",
        "roleCollection": "Extension Developer"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "CPI_OPERATORS",
        "roleCollection": "PI Business Expert"
    }
]

map-roles.mjs

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import 'dotenv/config';

const { TOKEN_URL, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, API_URL, IAS_ORIGIN_KEY } = process.env;

async function getToken() {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'client_credentials',
        response_type: 'token',
        client_id: CLIENT_ID,
        client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET
    });
    const res = await fetch(TOKEN_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
        body: params
    });
    const { access_token } = await res.json();
    return access_token;
}

async function mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection) {
    const url = `${API_URL}/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/${IAS_ORIGIN_KEY}/attributes`;
    const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            Accept: 'application/json'
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            attributeName: 'Groups',
            attributeValue: iasGroup,
            operator: 'equals',
            roleCollectionName: roleCollection
        })
    });

    if (res.status === 409) {
        console.log(`Already mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (res.status === 404) {
        console.error(`Not found (check name): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (!res.ok) {
        console.error(`Failed (${res.status}): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    console.log(`Mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
}

const mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./mappings.json', 'utf-8'));
const token = await getToken();

for (const { iasGroup, roleCollection } of mappings) {
    await mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection);
}

Install the one dependency and run:

npm install dotenv
node map-roles.mjs

You'll see a clear log for every mapping: success, already exists, or failure with the exact entry so you can investigate.

Bonus: Multi-Environment Reuse

Once your mappings.json is ready, deploying to multiple environments is trivial. Re-target the BTP CLI and generate a fresh set of credentials for each subaccount:

btp target --subaccount <DEV_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# next subaccount 
btp target --subaccount <QA_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# and so on ...

What was an 8-hour cockpit exercise becomes a 2-minute operation per environment. Repeatable, consistent, and auditable.

 

Conclusion

The SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service API is one of those tools that, once you know it's there, you'll reach for regularly. The manual cockpit approach is fine for a handful of mappings, but as soon as you're dealing with real-world project complexity with dozens of role collections, multiple environments, repeated deployments, it simply doesn't scale.

The setup described in this post takes maybe 30 minutes the first time: prepare your mappings.json, configure the .env, run one test call to validate. After that, it's just a matter of running the script. For the customer that inspired this post, what would have been a full day of clicking was done before lunch.

If you give this a try, I'd love to hear how it works for you especially if you adapt the script or extend it to cover other security artifacts. Drop a comment below or reach out directly.

Further Resources

  • Download SAP BTP CLI – https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/#cloud
  • BTP CLI Documentation – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/account-administration-using-sap-btp-command-line-interface-btp-cli
  • btp create security/api-credential – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/btp-cli-command-reference/btp-create-security-api-credential
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub – Authorization API – https://api.sap.com/api/AuthorizationAPI/resource/Role_collections
  • Accessing Administration APIs of SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/accessing-administration-using-apis-of-sap-authorization-and-trust-management-service
  • Map Role Collections to User Groups – SAP Help – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/map-role-collections-to-user-groups

entry.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2:Setting Up Principal Propagation with OAuth2SAMLBearer Authentication
entry.content:
This is my 350th blog post, and I'm excited to continue sharing insights, experiences, and lessons learned with the community.

Introduction

When integrating SAP BTP services with SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 or SAP Service Cloud Version 2 or ESM, one of the most common requirements is ensuring that the identity of the logged-in user flows seamlessly from the source BTP application into the target SAP Cloud system. This is known as Principal Propagation.

Without principal propagation, every API call would authenticate as a technical/service user — losing all user context, audit trails, and authorization logic that depends on who is actually logged in. With it, the end user's identity is securely carried through, enabling fine-grained access control and meaningful audit logs on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud side.

This blog walks you through the complete setup using the OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow — the recommended approach for BTP-to-SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 connectivity.

How It Works — The Big Picture

User (logged into BTP app)
        │
        ▼
BTP Destination (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion)
        │  ── Generates a SAML assertion carrying the user's identity
        ▼
SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 Token Service
        │  ── Validates the assertion against the trusted certificate
        ▼
Returns an OAuth2 Access Token (scoped to that user)
        │
        ▼
API Call executed as the propagated user
The trust between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 is established by registering BTP's X.509 certificate as a trusted issuer inside the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant.

Prerequisites

  • Access to your SAP BTP Cockpit (subaccount level)
  • Admin access to your SAP Sales Cloud V2 / Service Cloud V2 tenant
  • Ability to call REST APIs on the tenant (e.g., via Postman, Bruno, or curl)

Step 1: Download the BTP Trust Certificate

  1. Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your subaccount.
  2. Go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust (top-right area of the Destinations page).
  3. A .pem certificate file will be downloaded.
  4. Open the file and copy only the certificate content — the block between (but not including) the header and footer lines:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIEXzCCA0...   ← copy everything between these lines
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

Keep this certificate value handy — you'll need it in the next step.

Step 2: Configure Inbound OAuth2 Trust in SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2

SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 needs to know about BTP as a trusted SAML assertion issuer. This is done via a dedicated IAM Service REST API on your tenant.

Important restriction: Only one OAuth2 SAML Bearer Inbound Configuration can exist per tenant.

2a. Check if a Configuration Already Exists

Send a GET request to check the current state:

GET <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
  • If a configuration exists with the same BTP certificate → you can reuse it as-is.
  • If a configuration exists with a different certificate → update it (Step 2b).
  • If no configuration exists → create a new one (Step 2c).

2b. Update an Existing Configuration (PUT)

PUT <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration/34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "<existing Id found in Step 2a>",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2c. Create a New Configuration (POST)

POST <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2d. Save the Response Values

A successful POST or PUT returns a JSON response like this:

{
  "value": {
    "id": "...",
    "grantType": "SAML2_BEARER",
    "nameIdType": "EMAIL",
    "spEntityId": "...",
    "audience": "<AUDIENCE>",
    "tokenServiceUrl": "<TOKEN_URL>",
    "clientId": "<CLIENT_ID>",
    "scopes": ["<SCOPE_ID>"],
    "clientAppName": "...",
    "certificate": "..."
  }
}

Note down these four values — you'll need them in Step 3:

Field Used As

audienceAudience in BTP destination
tokenServiceUrlToken Service URL in BTP destination
clientId → appears as CLIENT_IDClient Key in BTP destination
scopes[0] → SCOPE_IDScope in BTP destination

Step 3: Create the BTP Destination

Now configure a destination in your BTP subaccount that uses the inbound configuration values you just collected.

  1. Go to SAP BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations → New Destination.
  2. Fill in the following fields:

Property Value

NameYour choice (e.g., SalesCloudV2_PrincipalProp)
TypeHTTP
URL<Your SAP Sales/Service Cloud Tenant Host URL>
AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
Audience<AUDIENCE> from the inbound config response
AuthnContextClassRefurn:none
Client Key<CLIENT_ID> from the inbound config response
Token Service URL<TOKEN_URL> from the inbound config response
Scope<SCOPE_ID> from the inbound config response
nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

The nameIdFormat value tells the system to use the user's email address as the SAML NameID — this is how the user identity is matched on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 or ESM side.

Step 4: Configure Trusted Domains in SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management

As a final step, ensure that your SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant domain is registered as a trusted domain in SAP BTP's Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA/SAP Cloud Identity Services).

Refer to the official SAP documentation: Configure Trusted Domains for SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service.

This ensures that SAML assertions issued by BTP are only accepted by explicitly trusted target systems — an important security boundary.

Summary

Here's a quick recap of the end-to-end setup:

Step 1 → Download BTP X.509 Trust Certificate
Step 2 → Register certificate as Inbound OAuth2 Config on SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2
Step 3 → Create OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Destination in BTP using response values
Step 4 → Register SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 domain as trusted in BTP Auth & Trust

Once complete, any BTP application or service using this destination will automatically propagate the logged-in user's identity to SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 — without requiring users to re-authenticate or sharing technical credentials.

Key Takeaways

  • Principal Propagation bridges the identity gap between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2, preserving the real user context across systems.
  • The trust is certificate-based — BTP's signing certificate is registered directly in the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 IAM service.
  • The fixed UUID (34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667) is a well-known system identifier for this configuration — don't change it.
  • Only one inbound configuration is allowed per tenant, so manage it carefully across teams.
  • User matching relies on email address as the SAML NameID — ensure users exist with the same email in both systems.

Share to your colleagues or Have questions or ran into issues during the setup? Drop them in the comments below.

entry.title: SAP Key Management Service: Taking Control of Your Encryption Keys in the Cloud
entry.content:
How SAP KMS empowers customers to manage their own cryptographic keys across SAP cloud services and products

Introduction

In an era where data sovereignty and regulatory compliance are paramount, organizations moving to the cloud face a critical question: who controls the encryption keys that protect their most sensitive data? SAP has answered this question with the SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) — a service designed to put customers firmly in control of their data across SAP cloud services and products.

By managing their own encryption keys, customers decide exactly who can access their information. With SAP KMS, data remains inaccessible to any external party — including SAP. This represents a fundamental shift in how data sovereignty is maintained in SAP cloud environments.

This blog post provides an in-depth look at SAP KMS, its capabilities, the key management models it supports, and how it integrates with SAP’s cloud portfolio to deliver enterprise-grade data protection.

 

Why Key Management Matters in the Cloud

For enhanced security and data protection, customers require control over their cryptographic keys, empowering them to take a proactive approach to securing their data hosted on SAP cloud services.

The need for customer-controlled key management is driven by several factors:

  • Regulatory Compliance: Regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, and industry-specific mandates often require organizations to demonstrate control over their encryption mechanisms and keys.
  • Data Sovereignty: Organizations need assurance that their data cannot be accessed by unauthorized parties, including cloud service providers.
  • Risk Mitigation: Controlling encryption keys allows organizations to revoke access instantly, rendering data unreadable in the event of a breach or a change in business relationships.
  • Zero-Trust Architecture: Modern security frameworks demand that no entity — internal or external — is implicitly trusted. Customer-controlled key management aligns with this principle.

 

What Is SAP Key Management Service?

SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) is a cloud-based service that provides customers with a centralized and secure way to manage the cryptographic keys used to encrypt data across SAP cloud services.

The service enables customers to securely manage and control the encryption keys used to protect their business data, and helps ensure that encryption and decryption can occur only with their approval.

 

Core Capabilities

SAP KMS provides a comprehensive set of key management capabilities:

Capability

Description

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)

Import existing keys from external key management systems into SAP KMS FIPS 140-2 Level 3-compliant keystore

Hold Your Own Key (HYOK)

Register a key from an external keystore to keep the key material in the customer keystore only

Key rotation

Rotate keys on demand and re-encrypt top-level keys

Global or regional deployment

Deploy one or multiple SAP KMS tenants based on customer need

4+ eyes principle

Use workflows to secure all key actions executed by key administrators

Key wrapping

Wrap and unwrap data encryption keys for secure distribution across services

Flexible assignment

Flexibly assign SAP cloud solutions to customer keys

Access control

Role-based access, authentication, and authorization for key management operations

 

Customer-Managed Key Scenarios

SAP KMS supports multiple key management models to accommodate different security requirements and compliance postures. Each model offers a different balance of control, convenience, and operational responsibility.

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)

BYOK allows customers to generate a key externally and import it into the SAP KMS tenant. This model is suited for organizations that want to generate keys using their own certified hardware security modules (HSMs) while still leveraging SAP’s managed key infrastructure for daily operations.

Hold Your Own Key (HYOK)

HYOK represents the highest level of customer control. The encryption key never leaves the customer’s external keystore. SAP KMS is connected to the customer’s external key management system and uses the permitted key for cryptographic operations without ever storing or caching it.

  • The key remains under the customer’s sole control at all times
  • The customer can revoke access instantly by disabling the key in their external keystore

 

Key Scenario Comparison

Aspect

BYOK

HYOK

Key location

Generated externally, imported to SAP

Customer’s external keystore

Customer control

After import of the key, lifecycle within SAP KMS

Complete — key never leaves customer

SAP access to key

No direct access

No access — remote calls only

Revocation speed

Immediate via SAP KMS tenant

Immediate via external keystore

Best for

HSM-centric, flexible organizations

Maximum control & compliance

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Integration with SAP Cloud Services

SAP KMS integrates natively with a growing portfolio of SAP cloud services, enabling customer-managed encryption across the SAP landscape:

  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (coming soon)
  • SAP Datasphere (SAP Business Data Cloud)
  • SAP Credential Store (SAP Business Technology Platform)
  • SAP HANA Cloud (SAP Business Technology Platform)
  • More to come…

 

How SAP KMS Works: Architecture Overview

At a high level, SAP KMS operates within a layered encryption architecture:

  1. Data Encryption: SAP cloud services encrypt data at rest using Data Encryption Keys (DEKs) generated by the service itself.
  2. Key Encryption: The DEKs are encrypted (wrapped) using root encryption keys managed within the SAP service’s secure store (e.g., SAP HANA’s Instance Secure Store or Local Secure Store).
  3. Customer Master Key: SAP KMS provides the customer’s master key, which encrypts (wraps) the root encryption keys. This is the key the customer controls.
  4. Access Control: Without the customer’s master key, the root keys cannot be decrypted, and therefore the data remains inaccessible. Revoking the key immediately locks the data.

This envelope encryption approach ensures that SAP never needs direct access to customer data, while the customer maintains a “kill switch” capability to revoke access at any time.

SAP Key Management Service Architecture

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Security Foundations

SAP KMS is built on robust security foundations to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of key management operations:

  • FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Compliance: The underlying keystore infrastructure meets stringent federal security standards
  • Cloud-Agnostic Architecture: SAP KMS operates independently of the underlying hyperscaler, providing consistent security across multi-cloud deployments
  • Role-Based Access Control: Granular roles (Key Administrator, Key User) ensure separation of duties in key management operations
  • Comprehensive Audit Trail: Every key operation is logged for compliance and forensic purposes

 

Conclusion

SAP Key Management Service represents a significant step forward in SAP’s commitment to customer data sovereignty and cloud security. By enabling customers to manage, rotate, and revoke their own encryption keys, SAP KMS ensures that organizations maintain full control over their data — even in a fully cloud-hosted environment.

Whether you choose BYOK or HYOK for maximum control with keys that never leave your keystore, SAP KMS provides the flexibility to meet your security and compliance requirements.

As SAP continues to expand the integration of KMS across its cloud portfolio, organizations can confidently accelerate their cloud transformation knowing that their most sensitive data remains firmly under their control.

If you want to learn more about the new solution, actively engage with SAP subject matter experts and your peers, and stay up to date about the topic of SAP Key Management Service, join our community at our SAP Key Management Service topic page!

 

Further Reading

  • SAP KMS Help Page
  • SAP KMS Product Page
  • SAP KMS Topic Page

entry.title: The Hidden Security Habit Every SAP BTP Admin Must Master: Service Key Rotation
entry.content:
Introduction: the credential nobody owns

A service key is usually created in thirty seconds, pasted into a .env file or a CI variable or Destination or any 3rd Party applications, and then forgotten for years. That is exactly why it becomes one of the most dangerous objects in your SAP BTP landscape.

If you integrate anything with BTP from outside the platform (a local development machine, an on-premise system, a GitHub Actions pipeline, a low-code tool such as n8n), you almost certainly rely on service keys. They give you a client ID and secret, or a certificate, that unlocks a service instance: XSUAA, Destination, Object Store, Cloud Logging, SAP AI Core and many more.

This blogpost explains what service keys really are, why you must rotate them, and how to do it without downtime, using the cf CLI, the btp CLI and a small automation pattern you can drop into a pipeline.

What a service key is (and is not)

A service key is a set of credentials generated on demand for an existing service instance. It is meant for clients that live outside the platform. Credentials meant for an application running inside Cloud Foundry or Kyma are called service bindings, and they reach the app through VCAP_SERVICES or a Kubernetes secret. The mechanics are the same, which is why this post applies to both.

For an XSUAA instance, a key typically contains the following fields:

  • clientid and clientsecret: the OAuth 2.0 client credentials
  • url and uaadomain: the token endpoint host
  • xsappname, identityzone, tenantid: identifiers of the application and subaccount
  • verificationkey: the public key used to validate issued JWTs

Whoever holds the clientid and clientsecret can request tokens with the scopes of the service instance, from anywhere on the internet. There is no IP restriction and no user attached. The key is the identity.

Credential types

Many BTP services let you choose how a key authenticates. The choice decides how painful rotation will be.

Credential type

What you get

Rotation effort

Typical risk

Client secret (default, binding-secret)

clientid + clientsecret

Create a new key, replace the secret everywhere

A leaked string works until you delete the key

X.509 certificate

Client certificate and private key (mTLS)

Keys expire by design; re-issue before expiry

Needs the private key, not just a string

Instance secret

One secret shared by the instance

Rotation touches every consumer at once

Large blast radius

For X.509 on XSUAA you request the type when creating the key, with a short validity:

cf create-service-key my-xsuaa key-x509 -c '{
  "credential-type": "x509",
  "x509": { "key-length": 2048, "validity": 7, "validity-type": "DAYS" }
}'

Supported parameters differ per service, so check the documentation of the service you use on SAP Help Portal .

Why rotation is needed

A service key never expires on its own (unless you chose X.509 with a validity). Every day it exists, the chance that it has leaked grows, and you never learn about the leak until it is abused. Rotation puts a ceiling on that exposure.

  • Leaks are silent. Keys end up in shell history, screenshots, support tickets, Postman collections, Git commits and CI logs. A leaked key looks identical to a legitimate one in the logs.
  • People and projects leave. The developer who created a key for a proof of concept may have left the company. Rotation, combined with an inventory, forces someone to claim every key or let it die.
  • Blast radius. A key carries the scopes of the whole instance. Short-lived or frequently replaced keys limit how long an attacker can use what they stole.
  • Compliance. Frameworks such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 and internal security policies commonly require periodic credential rotation and evidence that it happens.
  • Proof that you can do it. The worst time to learn that rotating a credential breaks three undocumented consumers is during an incident. A routine rotation is a fire drill you run on your own schedule.

What it buys you in an incident

If rotation is a routine, a suspected leak becomes a normal operation: create a new key, move consumers over, delete the old key. If it is not a routine, you face a decision between a possible breach and a possible outage, usually at night.

Deleting a key revokes its client secret at the service, so a rotation also invalidates any copy someone made earlier. Tokens that were already issued stay valid until they expire, which is why short token lifetimes matter as well.

The zero-downtime pattern: overlap, switch, retire

The key point is that a service instance can have several keys at the same time. You never edit a key in place. You add a second one next to the first, and you retire the first only after every consumer has moved.

  1. Inventory. List the existing keys and find out who uses each one.
  2. Create a new key with a versioned or dated name, for example ci-2026-10.
  3. Distribute the new credentials to your secret store or CI system.
  4. Switch the consumers: redeploy, restart or let them reload the secret.
  5. Verify that the consumers obtain tokens with the new key and that errors stay flat.
  6. Wait a grace period, so that slow consumers (nightly jobs, a colleague's laptop) fail loudly rather than silently.
  7. Delete the old key. This is the step that actually closes the leak.

Two habits make this reliable. First, name keys with a purpose and a date (n8n-prod-2026-10), so age and owner are visible in a listing. Second, give each consumer its own key. If five systems share one key, you can rotate it only by switching five systems on the same day, and you cannot tell which of them used it last.

Hands-on: rotating a key with the CLI

Cloud Foundry (cf CLI)

Start with an inventory of the keys on the instance:

cf service-keys my-xsuaa

Create the replacement key and read its credentials through the API, which is more robust to script than the formatted CLI output:

NEW_KEY="n8n-prod-$(date +%Y-%m)"
cf create-service-key my-xsuaa "$NEW_KEY"

GUID=$(cf service-key my-xsuaa "$NEW_KEY" --guid)
cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings/$GUID/details" | jq '.credentials'

After the consumers have switched and the grace period is over, remove the old key:

cf delete-service-key my-xsuaa n8n-prod-2026-09 -f

For service bindings used by apps, the equivalent is to create a new binding and restart the app so it reads the new VCAP_SERVICES. A rolling restart avoids downtime:

cf restart my-app --strategy rolling

Other environments (btp CLI and Service Manager)

In Kyma or any non-Cloud-Foundry environment, keys are called bindings and are managed through Service Manager. The btp CLI exposes them: btp CLI

btp list services/binding
btp create services/binding --name ci-2026-10 --service-instance my-xsuaa
btp delete services/binding --name ci-2026-09 --confirm

In Kyma, the equivalent is a ServiceBinding resource that writes the credentials to a Kubernetes secret. Creating a second ServiceBinding and pointing the workload at the new secret follows the same overlap pattern. Command flags change between CLI versions, so confirm them with btp help before you script anything.

Automating rotation and storing the result

Manual rotation works once. A scheduled job works every time. The script below creates a fresh key, hands the credentials to your secret store, and deletes keys older than a grace period. It is a starting point, not a drop-in product: adapt the secret-store call and test it on a non-production instance first.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

INSTANCE="$1"            # service instance name
PREFIX="$2"              # key name prefix, e.g. n8n-prod
GRACE_DAYS="${3:-14}"    # how long old keys stay alive

NEW_KEY="${PREFIX}-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
cf create-service-key "$INSTANCE" "$NEW_KEY"

GUID=$(cf service-key "$INSTANCE" "$NEW_KEY" --guid)
CREDS=$(cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings/$GUID/details" | jq -c '.credentials')

# 1. Push to your secret store (never echo or log $CREDS)
#    e.g. vault kv put secret/btp/$PREFIX value="$CREDS"

# 2. Retire old keys of this prefix beyond the grace period
INST_GUID=$(cf service "$INSTANCE" --guid)
CUTOFF=$(date -u -d "-${GRACE_DAYS} days" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings?type=key&service_instance_guids=${INST_GUID}" \
  | jq -r --arg p "$PREFIX" --arg c "$CUTOFF" --arg n "$NEW_KEY" \
    '.resources[] | select((.name|startswith($p)) and .name != $n and .created_at < $c) | .name' \
  | while read -r OLD; do
      echo "Deleting expired key: $OLD"
      cf delete-service-key "$INSTANCE" "$OLD" -f
    done

Where the new credentials should live

  • A dedicated secret manager. HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or the SAP Credential Store service on BTP. Consumers fetch the secret at start-up or on a refresh interval, so a rotation needs no redeploy.
  • CI/CD secrets. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Jenkins credentials, updated by the rotation job through their API.
  • Not in Git, not in images, not in chat. Not even in a private repository, and not as a plain environment variable baked into a container image.

Run the job on a schedule, for example every 60 or 90 days, and make the grace period shorter than the interval. Alert when a rotation fails, because a silent failure is worse than no automation: it creates the false impression that the problem is handled.

The cleanest long-term step is to remove the shared secret entirely. Where the service supports it, prefer X.509 credentials with a short validity, or an identity federation flow such as OIDC trust between your CI provider and BTP, so that no long-lived secret exists to rotate.

Pitfalls, checklist and conclusion

Common pitfalls

  • Deleting before switching. Remove the old key only after you have seen the new one working in production.
  • Forgotten consumers. Cron jobs, notebooks and a colleague's local default-env.json break after the delete. Use the grace period and watch authentication failures.
  • One key for everything. It makes rotation a coordinated big-bang change and hides who uses what.
  • Cached tokens and clients. Applications that read the secret once at start-up need a restart, or a reload mechanism, to pick up the new value.
  • Rotating the key but not the access around it. A new key with the same wide scopes only shortens the exposure. Combine rotation with least-privilege scopes and role collections.
  • No monitoring. Check the audit logs and authentication errors after each rotation; SAP Audit Log service records management operations on service instances.

Checklist

  • Every service key has an owner, a purpose and a date in its name
  • One key per consumer, no shared keys
  • Rotation interval defined (for example 90 days) and automated
  • Credentials live in a secret manager, not in code or images
  • Old keys are deleted after a fixed grace period
  • Failures of the rotation job raise an alert
  • Short-lived X.509 or federated identity used wherever the service supports it

Conclusion

Service key rotation is cheap insurance. It limits how long a leaked credential is useful, it forces you to know who depends on what, and it turns an emergency into a routine. Create the new key beside the old one, move the consumers, verify, wait, delete. Put that on a schedule and the quiet backbone of your BTP integrations stops being its quietest risk.

entry.title: SAPAutoLogon: Connect KeePass with SAP Logon and SAP GUI
entry.content:
Introduction

Anyone who works with many SAP systems keeps logon details somewhere: system ID, application server, instance number, client, user and password. A password manager is the right place for the credentials, but the connection data is usually typed again by hand, or the session is started through SAP Logon in a separate step.

SAPAutoLogon brings both together. It is a free, open source plugin for KeePass 2.x that reads your SAP Logon configuration, fills the connection fields of a KeePass entry, and starts SAP GUI or SAP Business Client directly from the KeePass entry list.

  Importing a SAP Logon folder into a KeePass group.

What the plugin does

SAP tab in the entry dialog. The Add Entry and Edit Entry dialogs get an additional SAP tab. In Manual mode, which is the default, you enter the connection fields yourself and a status line tells you whether the entry is ready to launch.

 The SAP tab in Manual mode.

In Automatic mode a searchable list shows the systems from SAP Logon. Selecting one fills the fields, and every field stays editable. Direct application servers, logon groups with a message server, SAProuter strings and SNC are supported. If SAP Logon stores no client or language, the plugin fills client 100 and language EN.

  The SAP tab in Automatic mode, with the search box and the selected system.

The values are stored as normal string fields of the entry (systemId, applicationServer, systemNumber, messageServer, messageServerPort, group, sapRouterString, sncName, sncType, client, language and transaction). They are visible on the Advanced tab, and the database stays readable without the plugin.

Import from SAP Logon. The context menu of a KeePass group has the command Import from SAP Logon.

  The group context menu with the Import from SAP Logon command.

A window shows the SAP Logon folder tree with the number of systems per folder, a search box and a preview of what will be created. Subfolders become nested groups and systems become entries. Existing groups are reused, and entries that are already present are skipped and never changed. You can optionally set a default user name for systems that have none in SAP Logon. Imported entries receive the SAP logo as their icon.

  The Import from SAP Logon window.

Launching. The columns SAP GUI and Business Client in the entry list start the session with a double click. The same actions are in the entry context menu and on the shortcuts Ctrl+Shift+G for SAP GUI and Ctrl+Shift+N for SAP Business Client. SAP GUI is started through sapshcut.exe, whose parameters are described in SAP Note 103019, and SAP Business Client through NWBC.exe.

  Imported groups and entries with the launch columns.

Installation

  1. Download SAPAutoLogon.dll from the latest release on GitHub.
  2. Copy it into the Plugins folder of your KeePass installation.
  3. Restart KeePass.
  4. The SAP GUI and Business Client columns appear in the entry list automatically.

Requirements are Windows, KeePass 2.x, SAP GUI for Windows with sapshcut.exe and/or SAP Business Client, and SAP Logon for the system list. Without SAP Logon the SAP tab still works in Manual mode. If you used another SAP launch plugin before, remove it first. The plugin supports the KeePass update check under Help, Check for Updates.

Security considerations

Please read this section before you use the plugin with productive systems.

  • The plugin only reads the SAP Logon landscape files, including the shared landscape file, and never changes them or the registry. If the shared landscape is configured as a URL, it is fetched with a plain GET request. There is no other network access and no telemetry.
  • To log on automatically, the user name and the password of the KeePass entry are passed to sapshcut.exe as arguments. The password is therefore visible on the command line of the process while SAP GUI starts. This is how sapshcut.exe works, so decide for each system whether this is acceptable.
  • The optional default user name of the import is stored in plain text in KeePass.config.xml. Never enter a password there.
  • An import changes the database in memory. KeePass has no undo, so review the result before you save.

Source, download and feedback

  • Project page with screenshots: https://abgunes.github.io/SAPAutoLogon/
  • Source code and download (AGPL 3.0): https://github.com/abgunes/SAPAutoLogon

The plugin builds on the KPSAPLunch plugin by David Suchopar. I would be glad to hear which connection types and SAP Logon setups you use, so please leave a comment or open an issue on GitHub.

#SAP GUI, #SAPLogon, #SAPBusinessClient, #KeePass, #Security

entry.title: Integrating Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services Using a Custom SCIM 2.0 Adapter on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Recently, I was working on an identity provisioning requirement where we needed to integrate Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS).

The idea was simple: Okta would be the source of users and groups, and SAP Identity Provisioning (IPS) would take care of provisioning those identities into SAP Cloud Identity Services.

However, during the initial analysis, we came across an authentication challenge.

The Okta environment was configured to use OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt authentication for accessing its Management APIs. We needed a way for SAP IPS to retrieve users and groups while supporting this authentication mechanism.

After exploring the available options, I decided to build a small adapter using Node.js and host it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry.

The approach worked, and I thought it would be useful to share how I built it, the architecture behind it, and a few things I learned along the way.

1. Why Did I Need a Custom Connector?

SAP Cloud Identity Services provides various options for integrating identity sources and target systems.

For this particular requirement, we wanted to use a generic SCIM 2.0 source in IPS.

The challenge was that Okta's native Management APIs use a different API structure, and our authentication requirement involved OAuth 2.0 with a signed JWT client assertion.

I wanted to avoid using long-lived Okta API tokens and keep the authentication mechanism aligned with the existing security requirements.

So, instead of trying to make IPS communicate directly with the Okta Management APIs, I introduced a small integration layer.

The idea was to let IPS communicate with a standard SCIM 2.0 endpoint while the adapter handled everything specific to Okta.

This meant I could manage authentication, API calls, and data transformations in one place without making the IPS configuration overly complicated.

2. How the Integration Works

The overall architecture is fairly straightforward.

 

Here's what happens when IPS runs a provisioning job:

  1. IPS sends a request to the SCIM endpoint hosted on SAP BTP.

  2. The Node.js application authenticates the incoming request.

  3. The adapter obtains an OAuth access token from Okta if needed.

  4. It calls the Okta APIs to retrieve users or groups.

  5. The retrieved data is converted into SCIM 2.0 format.

  6. IPS receives the response and continues with its standard provisioning process.

One thing I liked about this design was that IPS didn't need to know anything about Okta's authentication mechanism.

As far as IPS was concerned, it was communicating with a SCIM-compatible source.

3. Setting Up Authentication with Okta

This was probably the most interesting part of the implementation.

For the Okta connection, I used OAuth 2.0 client credentials with private_key_jwt authentication.

Instead of passing a client secret, the application creates a JWT assertion signed with an RSA private key.

Okta validates the assertion and issues an access token, which the adapter then uses to access the Management APIs.

For this integration, the required scopes were:

okta.users.read
okta.groups.read

The token request goes to:

POST https://{okta-domain}/oauth2/v1/token

With parameters similar to:

grant_type=client_credentials

scope=okta.users.read okta.groups.read

client_assertion_type=
urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer

client_assertion=<signed_jwt>

The Okta service application also needs the appropriate administrative permissions to read the required identity resources.

Once the access token is available, the application can call the Okta APIs.

For example, to retrieve users:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/users
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

And for groups:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/groups
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

I kept the Okta authentication logic inside the Node.js application. This way, IPS only needs its own credentials to access the SCIM service.

It also makes troubleshooting easier because the Okta authentication and IPS authentication can be checked independently.

4. Building the SCIM Adapter with Node.js

For development, I used Node.js with Express.

The application essentially acts as a translator between Okta's Management APIs and the SCIM 2.0 interface expected by IPS.

The main endpoints are:

GET /scim/v2/Users

GET /scim/v2/Groups

GET /scim/v2/Users/{id}

GET /scim/v2/Groups/{id}

I also considered standard SCIM discovery endpoints, which allow clients to understand the capabilities and schemas supported by a SCIM service.

Mapping Okta Users to SCIM

Okta returns user information in its own JSON structure.

For example:

{
  "id": "00u123456",
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "profile": {
    "login": "john.doe@example.com",
    "firstName": "John",
    "lastName": "Doe",
    "email": "john.doe@example.com"
  }
}

But IPS expects the response to follow the SCIM schema.

So, the adapter maps the Okta attributes into something like this:

{
  "schemas": [
    "urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User"
  ],
  "id": "00u123456",
  "userName": "john.doe@example.com",
  "active": true,
  "name": {
    "givenName": "John",
    "familyName": "Doe"
  },
  "emails": [
    {
      "value": "john.doe@example.com",
      "primary": true
    }
  ]
}

These are sample payloads to illustrate the mapping.

The same concept applies to groups, where the adapter maps Okta group information and memberships into the corresponding SCIM attributes.

Another thing to consider is pagination.

Okta uses cursor-based pagination for its APIs, whereas SCIM commonly uses startIndex and count.

For example:

GET /scim/v2/Users?startIndex=1&count=100

The adapter needs to handle this difference so that IPS can retrieve the required records correctly.

For larger environments, pagination becomes particularly important, along with filtering, error handling, and API rate limits.

5. Deploying the Application on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

Once the basic adapter was ready, the next step was to deploy it.

Since I was already working in the SAP BTP ecosystem, Cloud Foundry was a natural choice.

There was no need to provision a separate server or introduce additional infrastructure.

I used a standard Node.js application structure with a Cloud Foundry manifest.

An example manifest.yml looks like this:

applications:
  - name: okta-cis-scim-adapter
    memory: 256M
    disk_quota: 512M
    buildpacks:
      - nodejs_buildpack

Deployment was done using the Cloud Foundry CLI:

cf login
cf target -o <org> -s <space>
cf push

After deployment, the application was accessible through its Cloud Foundry route.

The Okta domain, OAuth client ID, signing key and other configuration values are supplied to the application through environment-specific configuration.

For production, I would recommend using a secure secrets-management approach instead of storing private keys or credentials directly in source code.

6. Connecting SAP Identity Provisioning to the Adapter

With the application running on BTP, I moved to the SAP Cloud Identity Services side.

I created a source system in SAP Identity Provisioning using the generic SCIM system connector.

The important part was configuring the source to point to the Cloud Foundry application instead of the Okta API.

An example configuration is shown below:

Property Value

Source SystemSCIM System
URLhttps://<btp-app-route>/scim/v2
AuthenticationBasicAuthentication
Proxy TypeInternet
ResourcesUsers and Groups

The adapter was configured to accept authenticated SCIM requests, and the corresponding credentials were maintained in IPS.

From there, IPS could call the adapter, retrieve the SCIM-formatted identity data, and process it using the configured transformations and target system.

The advantage here was that the provisioning logic remained within IPS, while the adapter took care of communicating with Okta.

7. A Small Issue I Faced During Testing

Of course, the first test didn't go entirely as planned.

When I initially tested the connection from IPS, I received an HTTP 401 error.

The request was reaching the application, but the adapter was rejecting it.

Initially, I was checking the Okta OAuth configuration, but the issue turned out to be on the incoming SCIM authentication side.

After reviewing the Basic Authentication configuration and correcting the credentials, the connection worked.

This was a useful reminder that there are two different authentication layers in this setup:

IPS to the SCIM adapter: Basic Authentication over HTTPS.

SCIM adapter to Okta: OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt.

Once the first connection was working, I was able to validate that IPS could communicate with the deployed adapter.

The next important areas for testing in a production deployment are user and group mapping, pagination, membership handling, full provisioning runs, and retry behaviour.

8. What I Liked About This Approach

Looking back, there are a few reasons why I think this architecture makes sense.

First, it keeps the integration relatively simple. The adapter does one job: expose identity information from Okta through a standard SCIM interface.

Second, the authentication logic remains independent. If something changes in Okta's authentication requirements, the changes can be handled within the adapter without necessarily redesigning the IPS source.

Third, it's reusable. Although I built it for Okta, the same pattern could be used with another identity provider that exposes its own APIs.

And finally, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry makes it easy to host this kind of lightweight integration application alongside the rest of the SAP landscape.

That said, introducing a custom component also means taking responsibility for its maintenance, security, monitoring, and API compatibility. It's worth evaluating the available standard integration options before choosing a custom adapter.

9. A Few Takeaways

This was an interesting implementation because it involved more than just configuring an identity connector.

I had to work across Okta authentication, REST APIs, Node.js, SCIM 2.0, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, and SAP Identity Provisioning.

A few things stood out:

  • Understanding the authentication flow before starting the integration saves time later.

  • Keeping authentication and data transformation separate makes the solution easier to troubleshoot.

  • SCIM 2.0 is a useful standard for reducing dependencies on provider-specific APIs.

  • Pagination and group membership mapping deserve attention from the beginning.

  • SAP BTP can be a practical platform for building small extensions when standard integration options don't fully match a requirement.

Source Code – GitHub Repository

I've also made the connector's implementation available on GitHub for anyone interested in exploring the approach or building something similar.

The repository includes the Node.js SCIM adapter, Okta OAuth authentication handling, and SAP BTP Cloud Foundry deployment configuration.

GitHub Repository: Custom Okta SCIM Adapter for SAP Cloud Identity Services

Feel free to explore the implementation, suggest improvements, or contribute.

Conclusion

What started as an Okta-to-SAP identity provisioning requirement eventually turned into a small but useful integration project.

By building a Node.js-based SCIM adapter and deploying it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, I was able to bridge the authentication and API differences between Okta and SAP Identity Provisioning.

The adapter is not intended to replace standard SAP identity connectors. It's an additional option for scenarios where specific authentication or API requirements call for a custom integration layer.

I wanted to share this experience because similar challenges can come up when integrating SAP Cloud Identity Services with different enterprise identity platforms.

Hopefully, this provides a useful starting point for anyone working on something similar.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to share your thoughts or experiences with custom identity integrations in the comments.

 

Note: This article describes a custom integration approach. The example configuration and JSON payloads are illustrative and should be validated against the actual implementation before production use.

entry.title: Q3 2026: Quarterly Release Highlights for SAP BAIP Security and Identity & Access Management
entry.content:
Security is constantly evolving - and so are the ways we protect our SAP landscapes. What’s new in SAP BAIP Security and Identity & Access Management? From new capabilities to valuable enhancements, here’s your quarterly roundup of the latest updates you won’t want to miss.

For a complete overview of feature deliveries for SAP Cloud Identity Services, check out our list of all new feature announcements in the SAP Cloud Identity Services Release Notes on the SAP Help Portal.

SAP Cloud Identity Services: Agent identity and IAM for SAP Joule

Agent identity represents AI and automation agents in SAP Cloud Identity Services. Agents can authenticate, receive authorization, and be managed like human users while retaining agent-specific capabilities and security controls. You can find detailed information for administrators on the SAP Help Portal.

We also released the identity and access management architecture required for SAP Joule, including the requirement for a single SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant, SAP-managed provisioning, and global user ID assignment. Understand this foundation before you implement Joule to ensure consistent authentication and authorization across all connected SAP applications.

SAP Cloud Identity Services: SAP-managed SAP Cloud Identity

SAP Cloud Identity Services support both SAP-managed and customer-managed integration models, depending on who is responsible for maintaining and operating the tenant, application and provisioning configurations.

SAP-managed refers to a delivery approach in which SAP is responsible for key technical and operational aspects of the solution. This approach reduces complexity for you and provides a consistent, best-practice experience. SAP manages the software lifecycle, including provisioning, technical integration, monitoring, automatic updates, backups, and offboarding. Customer-managed refers to a delivery approach in which you are responsible for configuring and maintaining your tenants according to your business requirements. This approach allows you to adapt features and functionality to your specific needs.

Identity and access management for SAP BAIP

You can now safely switch an OIDC trust configuration of a BAIP subaccount to another SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant without losing user data, such as authorizations or user-related data in subscribed applications.

For more information, see SAP Note 3468982.

SAP Key Management Service: General availability

SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) is now generally available to all SAP customers. It enables the use of customer-managed keys to protect data at rest across SAP cloud products and the SAP Business AI Platform. With consistent key governance and enhanced auditability, SAP KMS helps organizations meet compliance and regulatory requirements while maintaining control over their business data in SAP cloud landscapes.

For more information, please check our product overview and the SAP Help Portal.

SAP Secure Login Service for SAP GUI: Quantum-safe cryptography

We now support quantum-safe cryptography for the communication protocol between SAP GUI and SAP NetWeaver Application Server for ABAP. We have extended the Secure Login Client to integrate quantum-safe cryptography into authentication protocols, and we have enhanced the SAP Cryptographic Library to support quantum-safe authentication for the Secure Network Communications protocol. This helps protect communication channels between SAP GUI desktop clients and SAP NetWeaver Application Server for ABAP. It also prevents quantum computer-based harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks on SAP GUI communications using advanced security measures and ensures long-term communication security by adopting state-of-the-art cryptographic protocols.

For more information on the SAP Secure Login Service for SAP GUI, check the SAP Help Portal.

Stay in the loop

Join the SAP Business AI Platform Security and SAP Cloud Identity Services communities to get updates, share feedback, and connect with others!
